## Abstract {.unnumbered}

Pension rules paying the highest of several indices ratchet pensions above earnings; we ask what an earnings-anchored rule removes. From April `{python} SWITCH` the UK's adjusted Triple Lock raises the State Pension by the highest of `{python} FLOOR`, CPI and what keeps its April `{python} SWITCH - 1` value relative to earnings. Its excess over its earnings path follows a Lindley recursion, so the gap from the triple lock grows only in earnings-led years after price- or floor-led ones. Replayed from April `{python} hw_first["first"]`, it removes `{python} pct(100 * G_HIST / Y_HIST, 0)` of the triple lock's excess, leaving the pension `{python} pct(hw_first["gap_pct"], 1)` lower in `{python} fy(LAST_HIST)`. In `{python} fy(FINAL)` it lowers State Pension spending by `{python} bn(c_g, 1)` on the Office for Budget Responsibility's (OBR) central path and `{python} bn(w_g, 1)` with the OBR's long-term premium on the triple lock only, `{python} pct(SHARE['wedge'][0], 2)` of spending, an upper bound on that share under the convention. Averaged over `{python} N_DRAWS` simulated paths with earnings growth `{python} SHIFT` points lower or higher, it saves `{python} bn(lo_g, 1)` or `{python} bn(hi_g, 1)`. Their model overstates how often earnings growth falls below `{python} FLOOR`; it and a second model of OBR forecast errors each failed a test fixed before we computed the scores it was judged on, so these are scenarios, not an expected value. The Department for Work and Pensions estimates £`{python} dwp_nominal`bn for Great Britain. With that premium, pensioner poverty after housing costs rises `{python} num(pov_w["pensioners_absolute_ahc"], 2)` to `{python} num(pov_w["pensioners_relative_ahc"], 2)` points.

**Keywords:** `{python} KEYWORDS`. **JEL codes:** `{python} JEL`.

## Introduction {#sec-intro}

Indexation rules set how pensions in payment keep pace with prices and earnings, and with them much of a pension system's long-run cost [@vidalmelia2009; @oecd_pag2023]. A rule that pays the highest of several indices each year is asymmetric: it passes on every year in which one index leads and keeps that gain in all later years. We ask which part of such a rule's excess over earnings an earnings-anchored rule removes, on which paths of the indices, and what we can report when the model of the indices' variation fails a test against past forecasts.

Since April 2011 the triple lock has raised the State Pension each April by the highest of prices, earnings growth and `{python} FLOOR` (prices measured by the Retail Prices Index (RPI) in its first year and by the Consumer Prices Index (CPI) since), except in April `{python} D.HISTORY["suspended_earnings_year"]`, when the law suspended the earnings leg (@sec-background). Because it takes the highest of three figures every year, a year in which prices or the floor run ahead of earnings raises the pension for good, and later rises build on the higher level. The Office for Budget Responsibility's (OBR) long-term projections assume that the triple lock raises the pension `{python} obr_premium` percentage points a year faster than earnings [@obr_lted2026], and it estimates that by 2029-30 the triple lock will have added `{python} re.search(r"£[\d.]+ billion", D.benchmark("obr_frs_2025")["figure_text"]).group(0)` a year to spending relative to earnings uprating since its introduction [@obr_frs2025]. We call the indexation floors of such rules guarantees; the Pension Credit guarantee, the means-tested minimum income for pensioners, is always named in full.

The government announced the adjusted Triple Lock on 29 September 2026, and the Budget of 28 October 2026 confirmed it, to take effect from the next Parliament: the triple lock applies to each rise through April `{python} SWITCH - 1`, and from April `{python} SWITCH` the pension also falls back towards its April `{python} SWITCH - 1` value relative to earnings after years in which prices or the floor beat earnings (@sec-two-rules). The Budget puts the saving at: "`{python} budget_saving`" [@budget2026, para. 1.29], citing the analysis of the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) [@dwp_uprating2026], and it recognises that the saving depends on the path of the indices: "`{python} budget_hard`" [@budget2026, Box 5.A]. We quantify that dependence. The Budget links the saving to funding a new settlement for older people, including personal care in England [@budget2026, chapter 1], and the OBR notes that "`{python} D.EFO_CARE`", so that the long-term effect of the two announcements together depends on that reform's cost [@obr_efo2026oct, para. 3.54]; we cost the pension change alone.

The adjusted Triple Lock keeps the triple lock's protection against prices and the floor but removes the ratchet: the part of the triple lock's excess over earnings that it keeps after earnings lead again. The adjusted rule still pays above its earnings path while an excess lasts, so its saving is less than the triple lock's whole premium over earnings uprating. We estimate its effect against the triple lock from `{python} fy(D.YEARS[0])` to `{python} fy(FINAL)` with microsimulation runs of PolicyEngine UK [@ahmadi2026] on the whole survey population, on the OBR's central path, with the OBR's long-term triple-lock premium applied to the triple lock only, and on simulated paths of prices and earnings.

The main result is a characterisation of which part of the triple lock's excess over earnings an earnings-anchored rule removes: the gap grows each year by the smaller of earnings' lead and the excess the adjusted rule still carries, so it depends on the order of the indices' leads and not only on their average (@sec-formal). Replayed on past inputs from April `{python} hw_first["first"]`, the rule removes `{python} pct(100 * G_HIST / Y_HIST, 0)` of the excess; this is the evidence that needs no model of the indices' future. On the OBR's central and long-term paths it removes all of it, by construction of a smooth path on which earnings lead in every April after the price- or floor-led ones. On the two simulated scenarios, whose model overstates how often the lead changes, the adjusted rule's average gap is `{python} pct(100 * SIM_G["minus"] / SIM_Y["minus"], 0)` and `{python} pct(100 * SIM_G["plus"] / SIM_Y["plus"], 0)` of the triple lock's average excess, and most of it comes from year-to-year variation rather than from the paths' mean; the failed test bears on that variation, the two failed models disagree on its size (@sec-c4), and our test does not license an expected value.

The paper makes two contributions. First, we characterise the gap between a max-of-indices rule and its earnings-anchored variant. The anchored rule's excess over its earnings path is a cumulative sum reflected at zero, a Lindley recursion [@lindley1952], so the gap depends on the running minimum of the cumulative difference between the indices, as a lookback option's payoff does [@goldman1979]. The identity is standard; its use here is the gap's yearly increment, $\min(\max(-d_t, 0), x_{t-1})$, with two corollaries: costings that enter the triple lock's excess as a smooth premium attribute all of it to the ratchet, and a lead for prices or the floor in the last year saves nothing. We add the exact condition for a positive saving, an upper bound by the smaller of the indices' cumulative leads and, for independent yearly differences, the expected gap from Spitzer's identity [@spitzer1956], which rises with the differences' variance when they are normal (@sec-formal).

Second, we test a stochastic model of uprating inputs against official forecast vintages with proper scoring rules [@gneiting2007; @scheuerer2015], under a pass rule whose thresholds we registered before the first scores and whose treatment of April 2022 and of a failed baseline model we registered after them, before the second scores [@casey2012; @olken2015] (@sec-test). The baseline model overstates how often earnings growth falls below the floor, the event that opens the triple lock's excess, and we show which way that error moves the cost of the adjusted rule (@sec-budget). A second model, built on the OBR's past forecast errors and registered before its scores, also fails, and the forecast record explains why neither can support a probability distribution of the saving (@sec-discussion).

@sec-background describes the triple lock's record and relates the paper to the literature. @sec-rules states the two rules, derives where the saving comes from and replays the rule on past inputs. @sec-method describes the data, the microsimulation, the paths of prices and earnings and the registered test. @sec-results gives the fiscal effects, the mechanism along single paths and the distributional effects. @sec-dwp compares the results with official costings, @sec-discussion discusses what they imply for costing such rules, and @sec-conclusion concludes and states the main limitations.

### The triple lock since 2011

@fig-history shows the rises actually paid in each April from `{python} first["year"]` to `{python} last["year"]`. RPI set April `{python} D.HISTORY_RPI_YEAR`'s rise, `{python} rate(rpi_row["paid"])`, under that year's up-rating order [@uprating2011]; the replay of the CPI rule gives `{python} rate(rpi_row["rate"])`. From `{python} D.HISTORY_RPI_YEAR + 1`, CPI set the rise `{python} words(counts["cpi"])` times, earnings `{python} words(counts["earnings"])` times and the floor `{python} words(counts["floor"])` times. In April `{python} susp_year` the law suspended the earnings leg, whose input was `{python} rate(susp["earnings"])` on today's figures, so that year's rise was CPI, `{python} rate(susp["cpi"])` [@ssuba2021]. Over the `{python} words(len(rec))` rises the pension rose by `{python} pct(paid_rise, 1)` as paid.

### Related literature

Automatic adjustment mechanisms link a pay-as-you-go pension system's benefits or contributions to indicators, so that its finances respond to demographic and economic change without new legislation [@vidalmelia2009]; @knell2010 shows how the choice of adjustment factor changes the return such a system pays, and @valdesprieto2000 shows which indexation rules keep a notional-account system solvent. The indexation of pensions in payment is one such link, and the OECD's review of the inflation surge since 2021 records how far different rules protected pensioners' purchasing power [@oecd_pag2023]. The triple lock takes the highest of three figures each year, and @portes2023 places it in the longer history of the State Pension's value relative to earnings. A rule that pays the higher of two growth rates and compounds the result has the structure of a path-dependent option. The triple lock's excess over earnings, the sum of each year's lead of prices or the floor over earnings, compounds a yearly local floor, as a cliquet or ratchet guarantee does [@hardy2003; @tiong2000], while the adjusted rule's gap depends on a running minimum of the cumulative difference between the indices, as a lookback option's payoff depends on the running minimum of a price [@goldman1979; @conze1991]. The adjusted rule's excess over its earnings path is a draw-up of that cumulative difference, whose distribution the literature on the maximum drawdown of a Brownian motion describes in continuous time [@magdonismail2004], and Spitzer's identity gives its expectation when the yearly differences are independent [@spitzer1956].

The option analogy connects the paper to the valuation of guarantees. @merton1977 values a loan guarantee as a put option, @lucas2012 argues that public guarantees and policies should be valued at market prices that charge for the risk they carry, and @geanakoplos2010 apply that approach to accrued Social Security benefits. In pension finance, @dejong2008 values the liabilities of a fund that indexes benefits only when its funding allows, an option embedded in the indexation rule, and @hoevenaars2008 value the transfers between generations that such contingent rules create. We measure the cost in cash, undiscounted and with no charge for risk, because official costings of uprating rules use that measure and we compare our results with them; a market value of the triple lock's guarantee would also need a price for UK earnings and inflation risk, which we leave aside. We use the option analogy for the structure of the payoff only.

The same guarantee also shares risk between generations. @diamond1977 sets out the framework for analysing social security, and @ballmankiw2007 and @gollier2008 show how a pension system can share risk between generations that cannot trade with each other. Indexation decides who bears the risk in a pay-as-you-go system's returns: @shiller1999 argues for designing social security to share income risk across generations, @bohn2009 shows how fiscal policy and benefit rules allocate aggregate risk between cohorts, and @auerbach2011 compare how sustainable unfunded systems with different adjustment rules spread demographic and economic shocks. The triple lock insures pensioners against years in which prices or the floor beat earnings, permanently and at the expense of later taxpayers; the adjusted rule keeps that insurance only until earnings catch up, and so moves the risk of a fall in the pension relative to earnings back to pensioners for a time. We measure the fiscal side of that transfer, not its welfare value.

Long-run projections of pension spending are uncertain, and stochastic projections of social security finances express that uncertainty as distributions over paths of demographic and economic inputs [@lee1998]. The OBR's fiscal risks and sustainability reports treat the triple lock as a source of fiscal risk and project its cost against earnings uprating [@obr_frs2025]; in the long-term scenarios of its 2026 Fiscal risks and sustainability report, as summarised in the October 2026 outlook, the triple lock accounted for around a third of the projected rise in State Pension spending as a share of GDP [@obr_efo2026oct, para. 3.48]. Central banks and fiscal analysts publish fan charts to show the uncertainty around a central projection [@britton1998; @celasun2006]. Researchers can test a model that supplies such a distribution against outcomes: probability integral transforms check its calibration [@diebold1998], a forecast should be as sharp as its calibration allows [@gneiting2007calibration; @mitchell2011], and proper scoring rules reward a forecaster for reporting its true predictive distribution [@gneiting2007], including for multivariate outcomes [@scheuerer2015]. Density forecasts of inflation and output are better calibrated when they allow volatility to change over time [@clark2011], which our model does not. Official fiscal forecasts have their own evaluation literature, which scores their errors and biases after the event [@leal2008] and finds official growth and budget forecasts optimistic on average, more so at longer horizons [@frankel2011]; we know of no earlier test of a stochastic model of uprating inputs against official forecast vintages before a costing uses its paths.

Static tax-benefit microsimulation applies the rules of the tax and benefit system to a representative survey of households, with behaviour held fixed, and is the standard tool for the distributional analysis of benefit reforms [@sutherland2013]; UKMOD is one such model for the four nations of the UK [@richiardi2021]. Such models can add behavioural responses to the static calculation, as PolicyEngine UK does for labour supply and for capital gains realisations [@policyengine_uk]. Dynamic microsimulation models instead project individual life courses, including pension entitlements, forward in time [@li2013]; DWP's costing of the adjusted Triple Lock uses one (@sec-dwp). The net saving depends on how many newly entitled pensioners claim Pension Credit, and take-up of means-tested benefits responds to the size of the entitlement and the cost of claiming [@pudney2006]; our runs hold each benefit unit's claim decision fixed. Pre-analysis plans fix a study's hypotheses and tests before the researcher sees the data, so that the researcher cannot choose results after the fact [@casey2012; @olken2015], and @christensen2018 review their spread in economics. They are rare in model-based policy costing, where the analyst chooses both the model and its evaluation; @sec-test describes the plan we registered and how it changed after the first scores.

## Policy rules {#sec-rules}

### The two rules {#sec-two-rules}

Under the triple lock the full basic and new State Pension rise each April by the highest of three figures: the CPI 12-month rate for the previous September [@ons_d7g7]; growth in average weekly earnings, whole-economy total pay, in May to July of the previous year [@ons_kac3]; and `{python} FLOOR`. ONS publishes both inputs to `{python} TENTH` point, and both rules here use them at that precision. We index each input by the April it sets: $c_t$ is the September CPI rate and $e_t$ the May–July earnings growth published before April $t$, and $f$ is the `{python} FLOOR` floor. Fiscal year $t$ pays the level set in April $t$.

The adjusted Triple Lock follows the triple lock to April `{python} SWITCH - 1`. From April `{python} SWITCH` let $L_t$ be the pension's level and $A_t$ an earnings path that starts at the `{python} fy(SWITCH - 1)` level and grows with May–July earnings, $A_t = A_{t-1}(1 + e_t)$. Then

$$L_t = \max\bigl(L_{t-1}\,(1 + \max(c_t, f)),\; A_t\bigr).$$

The pension never rises by less than the higher of CPI and the floor, and never falls below its earnings path. In April `{python} SWITCH` this rise equals the triple lock's, since the earnings path starts at the same level, so the two rules can first differ in April `{python} SWITCH + 1` and the saving in `{python} fy(SWITCH)` is zero on every path. As a modelling assumption we round any top-up to the earnings path up to the next `{python} TENTH` points, so the pension never ends below that path; a top-up therefore leaves the pension at most `{python} TENTH`% above its earnings path, and the margin does not accumulate, because the rule sets each top-up afresh against $A_t$.

The Budget states the rule: from April `{python} SWITCH` the State Pension rises "`{python} budget_rule`" [@budget2026, para. 5.23 and Box 5.A], and adds that "`{python} budget_ratchet`" [@budget2026, chapter 1]. Its wording fixes the anchor: the pension's value relative to earnings "as reached in April `{python} SWITCH - 1`". DWP says the same in other words: "`{python} dwp_over_time`" [@dwp_uprating2026]. Two choices remain ours. The rule uses the triple lock's measures, September CPI and May–July earnings, and we round the top-up up, as above.

DWP published its analysis on the day the government announced the change [@dwp_uprating2026]. The OBR writes that its estimates of the change "depend critically on the order, level and covariation of wage growth and inflation over time" [@obr_efo2026oct, para. 3.53]. The rule would need primary legislation, because section 150A of the Social Security Administration Act 1992 requires the basic and new State Pension, and the Pension Credit standard minimum guarantee, to rise at least in line with earnings [@ssaa1992_s150a], with a corresponding order in Northern Ireland under section 132A of the Social Security Administration (Northern Ireland) Act 1992 [@ssaani1992_s132a]. In a year when the adjusted Triple Lock returns towards its earnings path, it rises by less than earnings growth. The suspension of the earnings leg for April 2022 also needed an Act [@ssuba2021]. @tbl-paths counts such Aprils on each path run through the microsimulation.

### Where the saving comes from

```{python}
ex2 = D.stylised_example()
(c1, e1), (c2, e2) = D.STYLISED
x1 = math.log((1 + max(c1, D.FLOOR)) / (1 + e1))  # the adjusted rule's excess over its earnings path after year one
d2 = math.log(1 + max(c2, D.FLOOR)) - math.log(1 + e2)


def gap_of(ds):
    """G after a run of yearly log differences d_t, from the recursions of the formal statement."""
    x = y = 0.0
    for d in ds:
        y += max(d, 0.0)
        x = max(x + d, 0.0)
    return y - x


# A spread that lowers the gap: around d = (+a, -a), the earnings-led year's difference spread by a either way.
SPREAD_A = 0.02
SPREAD_BASE = gap_of((SPREAD_A, -SPREAD_A))
SPREAD_LOW, SPREAD_HIGH = gap_of((SPREAD_A, 0.0)), gap_of((SPREAD_A, -2 * SPREAD_A))
```

When earnings lead, both rules give the same rise. The rules part only after a year in which the higher of CPI and `{python} FLOOR` beats earnings. Both pay that higher figure, but it lifts the adjusted Triple Lock above its earnings path. When earnings lead again, the triple lock rises with earnings from the higher level, while the adjusted Triple Lock rises only by the higher of CPI and the floor until its earnings path catches up. Under the triple lock each such rise stays in the pension's level; under the adjusted rule the level returns to its earnings path over the following years.

A two-year example shows the arithmetic. Suppose CPI is `{python} rate(c1, 0)` and earnings growth `{python} rate(e1, 0)` in the first year, then CPI `{python} rate(c2, 0)` and earnings `{python} rate(e2, 0)`. The triple lock rises by `{python} rate(c1, 0)` and then `{python} rate(e2, 0)`, `{python} rate(ex2["tl"], 2)` in all. The adjusted Triple Lock also rises by `{python} rate(c1, 0)` in the first year, which leaves it `{python} points(x1, 2)` log points above its earnings path, and then by the floor, `{python} FLOOR`, `{python} rate(ex2["plan"], 2)` in all. In the second year earnings lead by `{python} points(-d2, 2)` log points, less than the excess, so the whole lead becomes the gap: the adjusted rule ends `{python} rate(ex2["gap"], 1)` below the triple lock (`{python} points(ex2["points"], 2)` points less cumulative growth). The next subsection states this in general.

### A formal statement {#sec-formal}

Write $m_t = \max(c_t, f)$ for the higher of CPI and the floor that applies in April $t$, and $T_0$ for April `{python} SWITCH - 1`, the last rise under the triple lock alone. With $P_t$ the triple lock's level and $L_t$ and $A_t$ as above,

$$P_t = P_{t-1}\,\bigl(1 + \max(m_t, e_t)\bigr), \qquad L_t = \max\bigl(L_{t-1}\,(1 + m_t),\; A_t\bigr), \qquad A_t = A_{t-1}\,(1 + e_t),$$
with $P_{T_0} = L_{T_0} = A_{T_0}$. Let $d_t = \ln(1 + m_t) - \ln(1 + e_t)$, positive in a year in which CPI or the floor beats earnings, and measure each rule's level against the earnings path, $y_t = \ln(P_t / A_t)$ and $x_t = \ln(L_t / A_t)$. Then

$$y_t = y_{t-1} + \max(d_t, 0), \qquad x_t = \max(x_{t-1} + d_t,\; 0), \qquad y_{T_0} = x_{T_0} = 0.$$
The triple lock accumulates every positive $d_t$, while the adjusted rule's $x_t$ is a cumulative sum reflected at zero, a Lindley recursion [@lindley1952]. With $D_t = \sum_{s = T_0 + 1}^{t} d_s$ and $D_{T_0} = 0$, the log gap between the rules, $G_t = y_t - x_t$, is
$$G_t = \sum_{s = T_0 + 1}^{t} \max(-d_s, 0) + \min_{T_0 \le s \le t} D_s, \qquad \Delta G_t = G_t - G_{t-1} = \min\bigl(\max(-d_t, 0),\; x_{t-1}\bigr) \ge 0,$$
and
$$0 \le G_t \le \min\Bigl(\sum_{s = T_0 + 1}^{t} \max(d_s, 0),\; \sum_{s = T_0 + 1}^{t} \max(-d_s, 0)\Bigr).$$

**Proposition 1.** The gap never falls, and it grows only in a year in which earnings lead while the adjusted rule is still above its earnings path, by the smaller of earnings' lead and the remaining excess. The gap after April $t$ is positive if and only if some year $s \le t$ in which prices or the floor lead ($d_s > 0$) is followed by a later year $r \le t$ in which earnings lead ($d_r < 0$). In particular the gap is zero on any path on which earnings lead in every year and on any path on which they never lead, and a lead for prices or the floor in the final year alone gives no saving. @sec-proof gives the proof.

Because $G_t \ge 0$ on every path, a path on which earnings lead in every year after the switch gives the smallest possible saving, zero. A path close to that, such as the OBR's central path, gives a saving close to zero, and a distribution of paths with changes of lead gives a positive average. Proposition 1 does not say that variation around a given path raises the saving above that path's own. The increment is concave in $d_t$ in a year in which earnings lead, so a spread of that year's difference can lower the gap: on the path $d = (a, -a)$ with $a$ = `{python} points(SPREAD_A, 0)` log points the gap is `{python} points(SPREAD_BASE, 0)` log points, and spreading the second year's difference by $a$ either way, with equal weight, gives gaps of `{python} points(SPREAD_LOW, 0)` and `{python} points(SPREAD_HIGH, 0)`, an average of `{python} points((SPREAD_LOW + SPREAD_HIGH) / 2, 0)`. Under independent differences, by contrast, the expected gap rises with their variance (Proposition 2); the counter-example needs a spread specific to one path. For any model of the inputs the bound above gives $\mathrm{E}[G_t] \le \min\bigl(\mathrm{E}[y_t],\, \mathrm{E}[\sum_s \max(-d_s, 0)]\bigr)$. The increment also says when the saving appears: larger earnings leads use up the excess $x_{t-1}$ faster, so higher earnings growth after a year of high inflation brings the saving forward.

**Proposition 2.** If the yearly differences $d_t$ are independent and identically distributed, then with $D_k = d_{T_0 + 1} + \dots + d_{T_0 + k}$ the expected excess and gap after $n$ rises are
$$\mathrm{E}[y_{T_0 + n}] = n\,\mathrm{E}[d^{+}], \qquad \mathrm{E}[G_{T_0 + n}] = \sum_{k=1}^{n} \Bigl(\mathrm{E}[d^{+}] - \tfrac{1}{k}\,\mathrm{E}[(D_k)^{+}]\Bigr).$$
If they are normal with mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $\sigma$, the expected gap is zero at $\sigma = 0$ and does not fall as $\sigma$ rises, for every $\mu$. @sec-proof gives the proof, which rests on Spitzer's identity [@spitzer1956].

Proposition 2 gives a check that needs no simulation, though persistence in $d_t$, such as runs of earnings-led years, and a mean that changes from year to year are outside it. At the mean and standard deviation of $d_t$ on the replay's inputs from April `{python} hw_first["first"]` to April `{python} LAST_HIST` (`{python} points(H_MU, 2)` and `{python} points(H_SD, 2)` log points) it gives an expected gap of `{python} points(SP_H[0], 2)` log points over those `{python} words(len(HD))` Aprils and an expected excess of `{python} points(SP_H[1], 2)`, against `{python} points(G_HIST, 2)` and `{python} points(Y_HIST, 2)` on the replay itself (@sec-past). At the pooled mean and standard deviation of $d_t$ on each earnings scenario's paths from April `{python} SWITCH` it gives `{python} points(SP_S["minus"][0], 2)` and `{python} points(SP_S["plus"][0], 2)` log points by `{python} fy(FINAL)`, against path averages of `{python} points(SIM_G["minus"], 2)` and `{python} points(SIM_G["plus"], 2)` (@sec-budget), and expected excesses of `{python} points(SP_S["minus"][1], 2)` and `{python} points(SP_S["plus"][1], 2)` against `{python} points(SIM_Y["minus"], 2)` and `{python} points(SIM_Y["plus"], 2)`.

The gross saving in a fiscal year is the difference in basic and new State Pension paid,

$$S^{g}_t = \sum_i w_{it}\,\bigl(b^{\mathrm{TL}}_{it} - b^{\mathrm{A}}_{it}\bigr) \approx \bigl(1 - e^{-G_t}\bigr)\, B^{\mathrm{TL}}_t,$$
where $w_{it}$ is the survey weight of person $i$, $b_{it}$ their basic or new State Pension under each rule and $B^{\mathrm{TL}}_t$ total spending on both under the triple lock; the approximation is exact, up to rounding, when each person's amount is a fixed share of the full rate. The net saving is the change in the government's direct budget balance, $S^{n}_t = \sum_h w_{ht}\,(\tau^{\mathrm{A}}_{ht} - \tau^{\mathrm{TL}}_{ht})$, where $w_{ht}$ is the weight of household $h$ and $\tau_{ht}$ the direct taxes it pays less the benefits it receives, State Pension included. The rounding of the top-up to the earnings path adds a small non-negative term to $x_t$, so the identities, and the proposition's "if and only if", hold for the unrounded rule; in the model runs a rounded top-up can leave a small excess that a later earnings-led year turns into gap. On the paths run through the microsimulation the rounding changes $G_t$ in `{python} fy(FINAL)` by at most `{python} points(ROUND_MAX, 2)` log points.

### The rule on past inputs {#sec-past}

```{python}
first_group = next(g for g in D.history_groups() if g["changes"])
unchanged = [g for g in D.history_groups() if not g["changes"]]
past_weekly = first_group["model"]["counterfactual_weekly"]["new_state_pension"][str(LAST_HIST)]
actual_weekly = first_group["model"]["actual_weekly"]["new_state_pension"][str(LAST_HIST)]
past_saving = first_group["model"]["saving_bn"][str(LAST_HIST)]
spike = max(rec, key=lambda r: r["cpi"])
replay = D.ENVELOPE["last_decade_replay"]
replay_gap = 100 * (1 - replay["counterfactual"]["level_ratio"][str(LAST_HIST)])
# The OBR's replay statistic is an average over all years of the payment gap; the same average on ours, from the
# earliest start that changes anything to the last April.
avg_years = [y for y in D.HISTORY["years"] if y >= hw_first["first"]]
avg_gap = sum(100 * (1 - first_group["ratio"][str(y)]) for y in avg_years) / len(avg_years)
```

We can check the decomposition on inputs that have already occurred, with no model of their future path. The replay uses today's revised ONS figures, so that both rules see the same inputs. It differs from the rise paid in April `{python} listing([r["year"] for r in differ_hist])`, by `{python} TENTH` to `{python} num(max(abs(100 * (r["rate"] - r["paid"])) for r in differ_hist), 1)` points, because ONS has since revised the earnings figures, and in April `{python} D.HISTORY_RPI_YEAR`, which RPI set. In April `{python} susp_year` (@sec-background) the replay's earnings path grows by that year's CPI, `{python} rate(susp["cpi"])`, the figure the rise followed, rather than by the published earnings figure. On the replay the triple lock rose `{python} pct(rise["triple_lock"], 1)`, against `{python} pct(rise["earnings"], 1)` for earnings alone and `{python} pct(rise["cpi"], 1)` for prices alone, which leaves it `{python} pct(above_earn, 1)` above where an earnings link alone would have taken it.

@tbl-past and @fig-past replay the adjusted Triple Lock on today's figures from each earlier April. Had it started in `{python} first_group["label"]`, its level in `{python} fy(LAST_HIST)` would be `{python} pct(hw_first["gap_pct"], 1)` below the triple lock's on the same inputs. Applied to the full new State Pension actually paid, `{python} gbp(52 * actual_weekly)` a year, that would be `{python} gbp(52 * past_weekly)`. Most of the difference follows April `{python} spike["year"]`, when September CPI of `{python} rate(spike["cpi"])` set a rise `{python} points(spike["cpi"] - spike["earnings"], 1)` points above earnings growth of `{python} rate(spike["earnings"])`; the gap opened in the earnings-led Aprils after it, as the increment formula says. From that start, the triple lock's log excess over its earnings path is $y_t$ = `{python} points(Y_HIST, 2)` log points. That is more than the `{python} pct(above_earn, 1)` above, which starts in April `{python} first["year"]` and counts April `{python} susp_year` at published earnings, while this earnings path grows by CPI in that April. The adjusted rule removes $G_t$ = `{python} points(G_HIST, 2)` log points of it, or `{python} pct(100 * G_HIST / Y_HIST, 0)`; the rest is the excess it still carries. Started in `{python} listing([g["label"] for g in unchanged], "or")`, the rule would have paid the same as the triple lock every year, because earnings have led in every April since. In full model runs, State Pension spending in `{python} fy(LAST_HIST)` would have been `{python} bn(past_saving["gross"], 1)` lower, and the government `{python} bn(past_saving["net"], 1)` better off once tax and benefits respond. Averaged over the Aprils from `{python} hw_first["first"]` to `{python} LAST_HIST`, the pension would have been `{python} pct(avg_gap, 1)` below the triple lock.

## Data and method {#sec-method}

### Model and data {#sec-model}

We compute every saving and household figure for a given path by running PolicyEngine UK [@ahmadi2026; @policyengine_py; @policyengine_uk] on the whole survey population, once under each rule. Like the static models that @sutherland2013 describe, PolicyEngine UK applies the tax and benefit rules of each year to survey households. It can also add behavioural responses, each of which compares a simulation with a baseline. PolicyEngine UK builds a baseline for every simulation; our code removes it, so no response runs and behaviour stays fixed in every run. The step on the OBR's labour-supply elasticities changes the earnings of employees only, for the two eldest adults in each household, with its participation response disabled, and it leaves out people aged `{python} V2["lsr_excluded_from_age"]` and over, the self-employed and full-time students. A second labour-supply response, whose elasticities are zero unless a user sets them, has no age limit; like the response of capital gains realisations to tax rates, it is zero without a baseline. The State Pension is not withdrawn as earnings rise, so a lower pension would change the work incentives of younger household members mainly through an income effect. All runs use policyengine `{python} V2["policyengine"]`, which pins policyengine-uk `{python} V2["policyengine_uk"]` and policyengine-core `{python} V2["policyengine_core"]`, with the national Microcosm dataset for `{python} fy(2024)` published with it (`{python} count(V2["households"])` households, whose records are built on the Family Resources Survey) [@microcosm2026]. We use the Enhanced Family Resources Survey, version `{python} V2["efrs"]`, only for the check against DWP's caseloads (@tbl-coverage). A path's CPI and earnings growth replace the model's economic assumptions before the data load, so benefit rates, tax thresholds and earnings follow it, and every run checks that they do. Only the basic and new State Pension differ between the two runs of a path. Under both rules the additional State Pension rises with September CPI and State Pension age follows the law's timetable. We model pension-age Housing Benefit under current law. We give money in cash terms for the UK unless we say otherwise.

```{python}
hist_gc = D.HISTORY["cpi"]["2023"], D.HISTORY["earnings"]["2023"]
```

Three conventions shape the net saving. First, the Pension Credit guarantee rises with May–July earnings under both rules. That is the minimum section 150A requires, and neither the Budget nor DWP's analysis says how the government will uprate the Pension Credit guarantee under the adjusted Triple Lock, so we take the statutory minimum as the main case. In each April since 2022 the Pension Credit guarantee has in practice risen by the same percentage as the State Pension, as in April 2023, when both rose by `{python} rate(hist_gc[0])` against earnings growth of `{python} rate(hist_gc[1])` [@uprating2023]; in every earlier April from 2013 in which prices or the floor set the State Pension's rise it rose by less, by the basic State Pension's cash increase in April 2013, 2014, 2015, 2018 and 2021 and by about earnings growth in April 2017 [@uprating2013; @uprating2014; @uprating2015; @uprating2017; @uprating2018; @uprating2021]. If it rose by the same percentage as the State Pension under each rule, it would be lower under the adjusted rule, the Pension Credit offset would be smaller, possibly negative, and the net saving larger (@sec-net gives a lower bound on the effect). Second, the income tax personal allowance stays at `{python} V2['personal_allowance']` to `{python} fy(V2['pa_frozen_to'])`, as current law sets it, and then rises with each path's September CPI; from April `{python} SWITCH + 1`, when the rules can first differ, the full new State Pension is above it, so a lower pension means less income tax even for a pensioner with no other income. The Budget's Pension Tax Allowance [@budget2026, Table 6.1] lapses after April 2030, before the rules can first differ, and we assume no successor. Third, Pension Credit take-up follows the dataset's own claim decision for each benefit unit, so a household newly entitled under the adjusted rule claims only if that decision says it would; Housing Benefit and council tax reduction respond only for households already receiving them, and passporting from the guarantee credit follows actual receipt.

### The population in each year {#sec-population}

The dataset represents households in `{python} fy(2024)`, and each record stands for a person of its age in every year. Microcosm calibrates its household weights once, in `{python} V2["anchor_year"]`, and through that year every run uses the dataset's own weights. For later years PolicyEngine UK would scale every household weight by the ONS's growth in the total population. Our code replaces that step: in each year after `{python} V2["anchor_year"]` it rakes the `{python} V2["anchor_year"]` household weights, by a bounded calibration that minimises their relative entropy and keeps each weight between `{python} num(D.RAKE_BOUNDS[0], 1)` and `{python} num(D.RAKE_BOUNDS[1], 0)` times its `{python} V2["anchor_year"]` value. The weighted number of people in each of `{python} count(D.RAKE_CELLS)` age and sex cells (five-year bands under `{python} D.RAKE_SINGLE[0]`, single years from `{python} D.RAKE_SINGLE[0]` to `{python} D.RAKE_SINGLE[1]`, then `{python} D.RAKE_OLD[0][0]` to `{python} D.RAKE_OLD[0][1] - 1`, `{python} D.RAKE_OLD[1][0]` to `{python} D.RAKE_OLD[1][1] - 1` and `{python} D.RAKE_OLD[2][0]` and over) then grows from its `{python} V2["anchor_year"]` level as in the ONS's 2024-based population projection, with each fiscal year taking three quarters of the mid-year population of its first year and a quarter of the next [@ons_npp2024]. The rake targets age and sex only and recalibrates no other total, such as incomes, benefit caseloads or the number of households. The dataset does not top-code ages, so we keep every recorded age. Each person's State Pension type follows from the date of birth that their age implies in each year: those who reach State Pension age before 6 April 2016 are on the basic State Pension, later cohorts on the new one [@pa2014]. A record of a given age therefore moves from the basic to the new State Pension as later cohorts reach that age. We do not simulate deaths, migration or contribution histories, and the dataset leaves out pensioners abroad. Records carried forward from today's pensioners may understate the entitlements of people reaching State Pension age in the 2030s, most of whom will have spent their whole working lives under the new State Pension.

### Paths of prices and earnings {#sec-paths-method}

```{python}
cp = D.CENTRAL["path"]
a27 = cp["april_2027_inputs"]
stat_src = cp["statutory_source"]
q_years = [int(y) + 1 for y, s in stat_src.items() if s == "efo_quarterly"]
cal_src = cp["calendar_source"]
efo_years = [int(y) for y, s in cal_src.items() if s == "efo_calendar"]
sim_switch = D.TRAJ["models"]["boot"]["switches_per_year"]
MINUS_SHIFT = D.MINUS + SHIFT
```

The OBR central path uses the OBR's October 2026 Economic and fiscal outlook (EFO), published with the Budget, for calendar years to `{python} efo_years[-1]` [@obr_efo2026oct], and the OBR's March 2026 long-term economic determinants after that [@obr_lted2026], which the OBR describes as a projection, not a forecast; the OBR published no long-term determinants with its October forecast. We call the combination the OBR central path. April 2027's State Pension rise uses the published May–July 2026 earnings growth, `{python} rate(a27["earnings"])`, and September 2026 CPI, `{python} rate(a27["cpi"])` [@ons_kac3; @ons_d7g7]. For the Aprils `{python} q_years[0]` to `{python} q_years[-1]` the inputs are the OBR's September-quarter CPI and April–June earnings growth; later Aprils use its calendar-year figures. The OBR forecasts average earnings on a national-accounts measure, which stands in here for May–July average weekly earnings. Both rules share these inputs.

The simulated paths come from a model of monthly changes in the CPI index [@ons_d7bt] and in average weekly earnings [@ons_kab9], fitted to data from 2000 to the latest published month, with the furlough months of 2020–21 left out. Each month's change depends on the previous month's changes in both series, with fixed coefficients; the shocks are past pairs of residuals drawn at random, so prices and earnings keep their joint variation, but the model has no periods of higher or lower volatility and no uncertainty about its coefficients. From the simulated months come both the statutory inputs (September CPI, May–July earnings growth) and the calendar-year growth the rest of the model uses. Every path is then shifted by the same smooth drift so that the average calendar-year growth matches the OBR's forecast in every year, while each path keeps its own ups and downs. The earnings scenarios move that drift by `{python} SHIFT` points a year from `{python} FROM`. Because the drift is the smoothest monthly path that meets every calendar-year mean, it also moves the months just before `{python} FROM`, so the scenarios' statutory inputs for April `{python} SWITCH` and `{python} SWITCH + 1` differ slightly (@tbl-inputs), and in April `{python} SWITCH + 1` in the opposite direction: May–July `{python} SWITCH` earnings growth averages `{python} num(100 * MEAN_IN['minus'][SWITCH + 1][1], 2)`% with lower earnings growth and `{python} num(100 * MEAN_IN['plus'][SWITCH + 1][1], 2)`% with higher. Holding both scenarios' earnings inputs for those two Aprils at the lower-earnings scenario's values, path by path, changes the average $G_t$ in `{python} fy(FINAL)` by at most `{python} points(max(abs(HOLD['G'][k] - SIM_G[k]) for k in SIM_G), 2)` log points and the `{python} fy(MID)` paired difference in the share saved (@sec-budget) from `{python} points(PAIR[MID][0], 2)` to `{python} points(HOLD['pair'][MID][0], 2)` points. We call figures like these, computed from the uprating inputs alone with no microsimulation run, rule arithmetic.

The shift matches calendar-year means only, so the statutory inputs that drive both rules sit off the central path's (@tbl-inputs). Over the Aprils `{python} FWD[0]` to `{python} FWD[-1]` the scenarios' mean September CPI is `{python} points(-off_c, 2)` points below the central path's, and their mean May–July earnings growth is `{python} points(-off_e["minus"], 2)` points below it with lower earnings growth and `{python} points(off_e["plus"], 2)` points above it with higher, so the two scenarios are not centred on the central path. The simulated paths also have earnings growth below `{python} FLOOR` in `{python} pct(100 * SIM_BELOW["minus"], 1)` and `{python} pct(100 * SIM_BELOW["plus"], 1)` of those Aprils, to compare with the shares the model expected and the test on past forecasts realised (@sec-test). These and the other averages over the sampled paths below are rule arithmetic on the stored inputs of the paths run through the microsimulation, weighted as the fiscal figures are; none is a fiscal result.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-inputs
#| tbl-cap: "The statutory inputs setting each April's rise: the OBR central path's, and the average over the simulated paths of each earnings scenario (rule arithmetic on the stored inputs of the paths run through the microsimulation, weighted as the fiscal figures are), %. September CPI is the same in both scenarios, which move earnings only; the smooth drift also moves the inputs for April 2030 and 2031, before the scenarios' shift starts."
body = []
for y in [y for y in D.YEARS if y >= SWITCH]:
    body.append([str(y), num(100 * CSTAT["cpi"][str(y - 1)], 2), num(100 * MEAN_IN["minus"][y][0], 2),
                 num(100 * CSTAT["earnings"][str(y - 1)], 2), num(100 * MEAN_IN["minus"][y][1], 2),
                 num(100 * MEAN_IN["plus"][y][1], 2)])
display(Markdown(md_table(["April", "CPI: OBR central", "CPI: simulated", "Earnings: OBR central",
                           f"Earnings: simulated, {MINUS_SHIFT}", f"Earnings: simulated, +{SHIFT}"], body)))
```

We count a change of lead as a change in the sign of a difference between consecutive Aprils, a tie keeping the previous lead, and give every rate per April transition, in two ways (@tbl-leads): on $d_t$, earnings against the higher of CPI and the floor, which drives the rule, and on earnings against CPI alone, which the test on past forecasts scored (@sec-test). The forward rate is above the backtested one, the record since 2011 and the longer record, in which earnings led in most years, and it is higher on the scenario whose earnings growth sits closer to CPI. We have not tested how it depends on the window we fit the model to.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-leads
#| tbl-cap: "Changes of lead per April transition. Against the floor: earnings against the higher of CPI and the floor, the difference the rule uses; against CPI: earnings against CPI alone, as the test on past forecasts scored it. Test on past forecasts: four-year windows, three transitions each. Simulated paths: the Aprils 2027 to 2039 against CPI, and from the switch against the floor. Calendar record: calendar-year CPI and average earnings. A dash marks a figure not computed."
def _central_cpi_rate():
    rows_ = D.path_rows(central)
    lead = [(1 if r["earnings"] > r["cpi"] else (-1 if r["earnings"] < r["cpi"] else 0)) for r in rows_]
    return D.lead_changes([-s for s in lead]) / (len(rows_) - 1)
_cl = D.path_leads("central")
_n_after = len([y for y in D.YEARS if y >= SWITCH])
body = [
    ["Test on past forecasts, baseline model's expectation", "–", num(bt_pred, 2)],
    ["Test on past forecasts, realised", "–", num(bt_real, 2)],
    ["Simulated paths, baseline model", "–", num(sim_switch, 2)],
    [f"Simulated paths, earnings {MINUS_SHIFT}", num(SIM_SWF["minus"], 2), num(SIM_SW["minus"], 2)],
    [f"Simulated paths, earnings +{SHIFT}", num(SIM_SWF["plus"], 2), num(SIM_SW["plus"], 2)],
    ["OBR central path", num(_cl["changes"] / (_n_after - 1), 2), num(_central_cpi_rate(), 2)],
    ["Record, April 2011 to 2026, April 2022 as in law", num(D.record_lead_changes(True), 2),
     num(gs["statutory_upratings_2011_2026_suspended_2022"]["switches_per_year"], 2)],
    ["Record, April 2011 to 2026, April 2022 as published", num(D.record_lead_changes(False), 2),
     num(gs["statutory_upratings_2011_2026_published_2022"]["switches_per_year"], 2)],
    ["Calendar record, 1989 to 2025", "–", num(gs["calendar_1989_2025"]["switches_per_year"], 2)],
]
display(Markdown(md_table(["Inputs", "Against the floor", "Against CPI"], body, "lrr")))
```

The fiscal averages for the earnings scenarios do not average every draw. The model makes `{python} N_POP` equally weighted draws of the baseline model; we sort them into `{python} words(D.N_GROUPS)` groups of equal size by the gap between the rules in `{python} fy(FINAL)` on those unshifted draws, plus a group in which the rules pay the same, and run `{python} N_DRAWS` of them through the microsimulation, allocated across the groups in proportion to each group's size and the spread of that gap within it, with at least two a group. Both earnings scenarios use these groups, this allocation and the same draws, shifted in opposite directions; each scenario's average is a stratified estimate of the mean over all `{python} N_POP` draws, computed from its own microsimulation runs with the groups' weights, and the `{python} fy(MID)` averages use the same groups. Its margin is a 95% Monte Carlo interval from a standard error that combines the sampling of the microsimulation runs with the sampling of the draws. The margin is conditional on the model and leaves out uncertainty about its coefficients. Since the gross saving is close to $(1 - e^{-G_t})B^{\mathrm{TL}}_t$ and rule arithmetic gives $G_t$ for every draw, a regression estimator on $G_t$ would narrow the gross margins; we keep the registered estimator.

### Testing the model on past forecasts {#sec-test}

```{python}
SR = D.SCREEN_RULE
c1 = D.R["uncertainty_ruling"]["c1_failure"]
c1_hits = re.search(r"coverage (\d+)/(\d+)", c1["common_failure"]).groups()
others_fail = [f for f in forms if f != D.PRIMARY_FORM and not forms[f]["passes"]]
fb_all = [D.C2["scores"]["A"]["suspended"][f]["floor_bias"]["mean"] for f in forms]
fallback = min(passing, key=lambda f: forms[f]["proper_score_ratio_geomean"])
APUB = D.C2["scores"]["A"]["published"][D.PRIMARY_FORM]
fb_se = A[fail_stat]["se_overlap_hac"]
past_pct = D.C2["past_years"][D.PRIMARY_FORM]["suspended"]["realised_percentile"]
gb_all = {f: D.C2["scores"]["A"]["suspended"][f]["gap_bias_pp"]["mean"] for f in forms}
gb_round = sorted({num(v, 2) for v in gb_all.values()})
gb_main = num(A["gap_bias_pp"]["mean"], 2)
gb_others = [f for f in forms if num(gb_all[f], 2) != gb_main]
```

An average over the simulated paths needs a model whose paths behave like the real inputs, so we registered a test on past OBR forecasts [@obr_hofd2026] before scoring any model; the analysis plan is public in the paper's repository (github.com/PolicyEngine/uk-triple-lock, file docs/METHOD.md), where the section that sets the rule used here is dated `{python} V2["c2_registered"]`. `{python} words(n_forms).capitalize()` versions of the model of prices and earnings enter the test: the baseline model (monthly steps, one lag, resampled residuals) and variants with two lags, annual steps, Student-t shocks and normal shocks. We fit each only on data available before each forecast, centre it on that forecast, and score it with proper scoring rules for each statistic and for the joint outcome [@gneiting2007; @scheuerer2015] and with the coverage of central bands. The scores cover the gap between earnings and CPI in each year, how often the lead changes, how often earnings growth falls below `{python} FLOOR` and the gap the two rules open after four rises. The test scores changes of lead between earnings and CPI, not the higher of CPI and the floor that the rule uses; the floor-years condition covers the difference. One test uses `{python} words(n_a)` forecasts, one a year from the `{python} D.origins("A")[0]` to the `{python} D.origins("A")[-1]`; another uses `{python} words(n_b)`, from the `{python} D.origins("B")[0]` to the `{python} D.origins("B")[-1]`. @tbl-rule gives the pass rule; we fixed the thresholds together, as a broad screen, before we saw any score, and the record of the rule gives no other basis for any one of them. The accuracy condition compares versions with each other, so the baseline model meets it by construction, and its calibration rests on the coverage and bias conditions.

The rule changed once, after the first scores and before the second, in two elements. It scores April 2022 as the law applied it (@sec-background): under the first rule every version failed when we scored April 2022 on the published earnings, which the furlough schemes had distorted, with `{python} words(int(c1_hits[0]))` of `{python} words(int(c1_hits[1]))` four-year outcomes inside each band (a seventh window closed only when ONS published September 2026 CPI). And it no longer lets another version replace a baseline model that fails: the first rule would have taken `{python} D.FORM_NAMES[fallback]`, which passes, so it would have authorised an average over its paths. Under the second rule only a passing baseline model supplies an average, and otherwise the analysis reports four scenarios: the OBR central path, the OBR long-term path, the historical replay and the paired paths with earnings growth `{python} SHIFT` points lower and higher. Every other element, including all thresholds in @tbl-rule, is as first registered (@sec-appendix gives the record).

With the data available at the October 2026 Budget, the baseline model failed one condition (@tbl-screen, @tbl-screen-bias). It expected earnings growth below `{python} FLOOR` in `{python} pct(100 * PRED_FLOOR, 1)` of the years tested on the `{python} words(n_a)`-forecast test, against `{python} pct(100 * REAL_FLOOR, 1)` in practice, on an event that sets $d_t > 0$; that error, `{python} num(fail_value, 3)`, exceeds the limit of `{python} num(fail_limit, 2)`. The `{python} words(n_a)` windows overlap and cover `{python} words(len(FY_YEARS))` distinct years of inputs, `{python} FY_YEARS[0]` to `{python} FY_YEARS[-1]`; earnings growth was below the floor in `{python} words(len(FY_BELOW))` of them (`{python} listing(FY_BELOW)`, setting April `{python} listing([y + 1 for y in FY_BELOW])`), against about `{python} num(FY_EXP, 1)` that the model's forecasts imply when each year takes the average of the windows that cover it. The verdict follows the registered rule, which compares point estimates with the limit; the test cannot separate `{python} num(fail_value, 3)` from `{python} num(fail_limit, 2)`, and the case for reporting scenarios rather than an average rests on the direction of the error, which the reweighting diagnostic of @sec-budget follows, more than on its margin over the limit. All `{python} words(n_forms)` versions share the error, with floor biases from `{python} num(min(fb_all), 3)` to `{python} num(max(fb_all), 3)`. The gap bias, `{python} gb_main` points for `{python} 'every version' if not gb_others else ('every version but one (' + num(gb_all[gb_others[0]], 2) + ')' if len(gb_others) == 1 else 'most versions')`, is the error of the OBR forecasts the paths are centred on: the OBR expected earnings growth to exceed CPI by more than it did. Given that mean, the excess of floor years implies paths that are too dispersed. The forward paths are also centred on OBR forecasts, so any systematic OBR error in earnings less CPI carries over to the scenarios unchanged.

The baseline model passed every other condition. The outcome fell inside its central 80% band in `{python} words(A["terminal_coverage"]["hits"])` of `{python} words(A["terminal_scored_origins"])` four-year windows and `{python} pct(100 * A["annual_gap_coverage"]["mean"], 0)` of annual checks, and its lead changes were close to those realised. On the published 2022 earnings, a sensitivity that does not enter the verdict, it expected `{python} num(APUB["predicted_switches"]["mean"], 2)` changes of lead per window against `{python} num(APUB["realised_switches"]["mean"], 2)`, and a gap bias of `{python} num(APUB["gap_bias_pp"]["mean"], 2)` points. The realised gap since 2011 sits at the `{python} ordinal(past_pct)` percentile of its paths. `{python} words(len(passing)).capitalize()` other versions passed and `{python} words(len(others_fail))` failed on the same condition, but the rule forbids promoting another version, so this paper gives no expected value.

After the baseline model failed, we registered a second model of the inputs before scoring it, together with what the paper would report if it failed: scenarios only, every score, and the model's distribution of the share of spending saved once, in an appendix, as the output of a failed model. The analysis plan holds the registration in a dated section, committed and pushed `{python} words(C4_MIN["code"])` minutes before we pushed the model's code and `{python} words(C4_MIN["scores"])` minutes before its scores; the public record shows that order and no more. The registration states its own limits: its hold-out is not chronological, so the pools include later forecasts; we designed the model after seeing every earlier score and the whole record of forecast errors; and it is the `{python} C4_NTH` version of the model scored against these forecasts. The second model centres each path on the OBR's forecast and takes its errors from the OBR's own record: the errors of the `{python} words(n_c4)` forecasts, one a year, from the `{python} D.origins("B")[0]` to the `{python} D.origins("B")[-1]`, one to four years ahead, measured as September CPI and May–July earnings growth less the OBR's calendar-year forecast for the same year. Each path takes one past forecast's errors for its first four years, continues with the four-year-ahead errors of the target years that followed, and adds a draw of the uncertainty in the average error. To score a forecast, the model holds out every forecast that shares a target year with it. It faced the same test as the baseline model, with three added checks on its central bands, and met every scored condition but one (@tbl-c4-scores); the past-years check could not be scored, because no record of forecast errors exists before 2011, and does not count as met. On the thirteen-forecast test its variogram score, a proper score of how the yearly gaps move together [@scheuerer2015], is `{python} num(c4_value, 3)` times the baseline model's, above the limit of `{python} num(c4_limit, 2)`. Across `{python} count(C4S["n_seed_sets"])` other sets of random seeds, computed after the verdict, outside the registration, the ratio runs from `{python} num(C4S["variogram_ratio_b"]["min"], 3)` to `{python} num(C4S["variogram_ratio_b"]["max"], 3)`, so the failure does not depend on the seeds; they vary only the second model's draws. It does depend on single forecasts. In a check also computed after the verdict and not registered, leaving the score of the `{python} c4_low[0]["dropped"]`, `{python} c4_low[1]["dropped"]` or `{python} c4_low[2]["dropped"]` out of both models' averages puts the ratio at `{python} num(min(d["ratio"] for d in c4_low), 3)` to `{python} num(max(d["ratio"] for d in c4_low), 3)`, and over all `{python} words(len(C4_D1["by_dropped_forecast"]))` single drops it runs from `{python} num(C4_D1["min"], 3)` to `{python} num(C4_D1["max"], 3)`. As with the baseline model's floor bias, the test cannot separate `{python} num(c4_value, 3)` from `{python} num(c4_limit, 2)`. In a split of that excess by forecast, also computed after the verdict and not registered, the forecasts from the `{python} c4_mid[0]["origin"]` to the `{python} c4_mid[-1]["origin"]` carry `{python} pct(100 * D.C4_VARIO["share_from_origins_2011_2015"], 0)` of its excess over the baseline model; their held-out pools hold mostly forecasts made from March 2017 on, whose errors include the years of furlough and of the 2022 inflation. On the seven-forecast test its floor bias, `{python} num(C4_FB, 3)`, sits below the limit of `{python} num(C4_FB_LIM, 2)`, but across the same seed sets it runs from `{python} num(C4S["floor_bias_a"]["min"], 3)` to `{python} num(C4S["floor_bias_a"]["max"], 3)` and exceeds the limit in `{python} words(C4S["floor_bias_a"]["sets_above_limit"])` of them, so the test cannot separate it from the limit. Under the registered rule the paper therefore reports scenarios, and @sec-c4 gives the second model's distribution of the share saved.

The test has little power. With `{python} words(n_a)` overlapping four-year windows, a model whose bands cover far less than 80% could still pass, and because the upper limit on coverage is `{python} SR['coverage_high']`%, the coverage condition cannot detect bands that are too wide. A third rule, the forward rule, applies only to estimates that use OBR forecasts published after this paper's inputs, and adds a test on outcomes not yet observed. It gives its first verdict after `{python} words(D.C3_YEARS)` years of outcomes, from `{python} D.C3_FIRST` to `{python} C3_REPORT`, so the forward rule can first decide whether we may report averages over the paths as estimates in October `{python} C3_REPORT`, when ONS publishes the last of those inputs, September CPI; @sec-appendix gives its power.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-rule
#| tbl-cap: "The pass rule for the test on past forecasts, April 2022 scored as the law applied it. A version passes only if it meets every condition on both tests."
rule = [
    ["Coverage", f"Between {SR['coverage_low']}% and {SR['coverage_high']}% of outcomes, yearly and after four years, fall inside the central 80% band"],
    ["Coverage, plausible range", f"The range of plausible coverage after four years includes {SR['wilson_contains']}%"],
    ["Bias in the yearly gap", f"Average error in earnings minus CPI at most {SR['gap_bias']} points"],
    ["Bias in lead changes", f"Average error in the number of lead changes at most {SR['switch_bias']} a forecast"],
    ["Bias in floor years", f"Average error in the share of years with earnings growth below {FLOOR} at most {SR['floor_bias']}"],
    ["Accuracy scores", f"No score more than {pct(100 * (SR['score_ratio'] - 1), 0)} worse than the baseline model's"],
    ["Past years", f"The realised gap since 2011 between the {ordinal(SR['past_low'])} and {ordinal(SR['past_high'])} percentiles of its paths"],
]
display(Markdown(md_table(["Condition", "Threshold"], rule, "ll")))
```

### Fiscal effects on four scenarios {#sec-budget}

@tbl-scenarios gives the reduction in State Pension spending under the adjusted Triple Lock, relative to the triple lock, on four scenarios, and @fig-scenarios the gross saving in each year. Two are single microsimulation runs. One is the OBR central path. The other, which we call the OBR long-term path, is our construction: it keeps the central path's inputs but pays the triple lock at the OBR's long-term triple-lock rate from April `{python} D.OBR_LT_FROM`, which phases in to earnings growth plus `{python} obr_premium` points, and applies the adjusted rule to the same inputs, so the premium goes to the triple lock only. The other two take `{python} N_DRAWS` simulated paths of prices and earnings, each run through the microsimulation under both rules, and move calendar-year earnings growth `{python} SHIFT` points a year lower or higher from `{python} FROM` (@sec-paths-method). We attach no probability to any of them, and the four do not form a probability interval. No model here supplies a probability distribution of the saving (@sec-test); @sec-c4 gives the second model's distribution of the share saved, with no cash figure.

On the OBR long-term path the saving is `{python} bn(w_g, 1)` in `{python} fy(FINAL)`, `{python} bn(w_n, 1)` once income tax and benefits respond (@sec-net). The adjusted rule's level on this path is the same as on the central path, `{python} gbp(52 * w_final["bp_weekly"])` a year for the full new State Pension in `{python} fy(FINAL)`, because the two runs share their inputs; only the triple lock differs. Earnings lead CPI and the floor in every April from `{python} earn_from`, so the adjusted Triple Lock returns to its earnings path and then follows it, and the whole of the triple lock's excess counts as saving ($G_t = y_t$). $G_t$ is the central path's gap, `{python} points(WS["central"], 2)` log points, plus the sum from April `{python} D.OBR_LT_FROM` of the log differences between the OBR's long-term triple-lock rate and May–July earnings growth, `{python} points(WS["rest"], 2)` log points, `{python} points(WS["total"], 2)` in all by `{python} fy(FINAL)`, and $(1 - e^{-G_t})B^{\mathrm{TL}}_t$ gives `{python} pct(100 * (1 - math.exp(-WS["total"])), 2)` of `{python} bn(B_w, 1)` in basic and new State Pension spending. Once the premium is fully in, the yearly difference runs from `{python} points(WS["late_min"], 1)` to `{python} points(WS["late_max"], 1)` points rather than exactly `{python} obr_premium`, because the OBR states its premium against national-accounts earnings and the rule pays it to `{python} TENTH` points against May–July earnings. The premium is the OBR's average allowance for years in which CPI or the floor beat earnings, and no path of CPI and earnings pays it every year.

This scenario bounds the share of spending saved from above under the OBR's convention, and only under it: the saving if the OBR's premium is paid in full and the adjusted rule pays none. Since $G_t \le y_t$ on every path (@sec-formal), the expected gap under that convention cannot exceed the premium's cumulated value, `{python} points(WS["total"], 2)` log points; because $1 - e^{-G}$ is concave, Jensen's inequality gives the same for the share of spending, `{python} pct(SHARE['wedge'][0], 2)`. The argument reads the OBR's premium, an arithmetic allowance of `{python} obr_premium` points a year, as the expected log excess $\mathrm{E}[y_t]$ from the April `{python} SWITCH - 1` anchor. In cash the bound need not hold, because the triple lock's spending base rises with its excess, and the two co-vary across paths. The OBR's own figures agree on the direction: its replay of 1990–2025 leaves the adjusted rule above earnings uprating on average [@obr_efo2026oct, para. 3.51], and its provisional long-term estimate leaves debt above an earnings-uprating scenario because it expects periods in which inflation or the floor would still bind [@obr_efo2026oct, para. 3.52]. Our simulated paths put the triple lock's excess above the premium (below), but they come from the model that failed the test, and the reweighting towards the realised frequency of floor years reduces $y_t$ as well as $G_t$.

The two earnings scenarios give `{python} bn(lo_g, 1)` and `{python} bn(hi_g, 1)` in `{python} fy(FINAL)`. They are averages over paths from the model that failed the test, carry the same failed condition, and are reported because the registered rule keeps them as scenarios whatever the verdict, not because they are more reliable than the average it withdrew. They are not a range around an unshifted case. The scenarios exceed the OBR long-term path because on the simulated paths the triple lock's cumulated excess over earnings is larger than the OBR's premium gives: its average log excess over May–July earnings from April `{python} SWITCH`, $y_t$ in `{python} fy(FINAL)`, is `{python} points(SIM_Y["minus"], 2)` and `{python} points(SIM_Y["plus"], 2)` log points, against `{python} points(EXCESS["wedge"][1], 2)` on the OBR long-term path. In April `{python} D.YEARS[-6]` to `{python} FINAL` the simulated triple lock pays `{python} points(SIM_PREM["minus"], 2)` and `{python} points(SIM_PREM["plus"], 2)` points a year above May–July earnings, against `{python} points(WS["late_mean"], 2)` on that path, so with higher earnings growth more of the excess arrives in the Aprils before the OBR's premium is fully in. The adjusted rule's average gap is `{python} pct(100 * SIM_G["minus"] / SIM_Y["minus"], 0)` and `{python} pct(100 * SIM_G["plus"] / SIM_Y["plus"], 0)` of the triple lock's average excess (a ratio of averages); the average of the share $G_t/y_t$ path by path, over paths with an excess, is `{python} pct(100 * RATIO_PATH["minus"], 0)` and `{python} pct(100 * RATIO_PATH["plus"], 0)`.

As shares of basic and new State Pension spending the two scenarios `{python} ('both save ' + pct(SHARE['minus'][0], 1)) if pct(SHARE['minus'][0], 1) == pct(SHARE['plus'][0], 1) else ('save ' + pct(SHARE['minus'][0], 1) + ' and ' + pct(SHARE['plus'][0], 1))` in `{python} fy(FINAL)`. Because they share draws, shocks and the selection of microsimulation runs, their difference is measured path by path: in rule arithmetic on the shared paths, the higher-earnings scenario's share exceeds the lower's by `{python} points(PAIR[FINAL][0], 2)` ± `{python} points(PAIR[FINAL][1], 2)` points in `{python} fy(FINAL)`, which cannot be told from zero, so most of the cash difference comes from the larger pension base that faster nominal earnings growth brings. Earlier the scenarios differ. In `{python} fy(MID)` the saving is `{python} bn(hi_mid, 1)` with higher earnings growth against `{python} bn(lo_mid, 1)` with lower, `{python} pct(SHARE_MID["plus"][0], 1)` against `{python} pct(SHARE_MID["minus"][0], 1)` of spending, a paired difference of `{python} points(PAIR[MID][0], 2)` ± `{python} points(PAIR[MID][1], 2)` points: larger earnings leads use up the adjusted rule's excess over its earnings path sooner, so the increment in @sec-formal brings the saving forward.

The scenarios differ from the central path in both the mean and the variation of their inputs (@tbl-inputs), so the comparison with the central path does not by itself measure an effect of variation. Rule arithmetic separates the two. On a single path through each scenario's mean statutory inputs, $G_t$ in `{python} fy(FINAL)` is `{python} points(SIM_DET["minus"], 2)` log points with lower earnings growth and `{python} points(SIM_DET["plus"], 2)` with higher, against averages over the scenarios' paths of `{python} points(SIM_G["minus"], 2)` and `{python} points(SIM_G["plus"], 2)` (@tbl-scenarios). The year-to-year variation around those means thus accounts for `{python} points(SIM_G["minus"] - SIM_DET["minus"], 2)` and `{python} points(SIM_G["plus"] - SIM_DET["plus"], 2)` log points, most of each scenario's gap.

The failed condition bears on these averages, and a diagnostic, not an estimate, shows which way. Reweighting each scenario's sampled paths by exponential tilting on their number of Aprils from `{python} FWD[0]` to `{python} FWD[-1]` with earnings growth below `{python} FLOOR`, so that the share of such Aprils equals the `{python} pct(100 * REAL_FLOOR, 1)` realised in the test, lowers the average $G_t$ in `{python} fy(FINAL)` from `{python} points(TILT["minus"]["G0"], 2)` to `{python} points(TILT["minus"]["G"], 2)` log points with lower earnings growth and from `{python} points(TILT["plus"]["G0"], 2)` to `{python} points(TILT["plus"]["G"], 2)` with higher. It lowers the average excess $y_t$ from `{python} points(TILT["minus"]["y0"], 2)` to `{python} points(TILT["minus"]["y"], 2)` and from `{python} points(TILT["plus"]["y0"], 2)` to `{python} points(TILT["plus"]["y"], 2)`. The effective sample sizes are `{python} num(TILT["minus"]["kish"], 0)` and `{python} num(TILT["plus"]["kish"], 0)` sampled paths against `{python} num(TILT["plus"]["kish0"], 0)` before the tilt (the `{python} N_DRAWS` runs carry unequal group weights). That tilt also raises the paths' mean May–July earnings growth over those Aprils, from `{python} rate(TILT["minus"]["earn0"], 2)` to `{python} rate(TILT["minus"]["earn"], 2)` and from `{python} rate(TILT["plus"]["earn0"], 2)` to `{python} rate(TILT["plus"]["earn"], 2)`. For the lower-earnings scenario no reweighting of the sampled paths holds that mean fixed, and the tilt moves it above the central path's `{python} rate(sum(CSTAT['earnings'][str(y - 1)] for y in FWD) / len(FWD), 2)`, so the diagnostic does not describe that scenario. For the higher-earnings scenario a tilt that holds mean earnings fixed lowers the gap from `{python} points(TILT_HOLD["plus"]["G0"], 2)` to `{python} points(TILT_HOLD["plus"]["G"], 2)` log points (effective size `{python} num(TILT_HOLD["plus"]["kish"], 0)`). Of that gap, `{python} points(TILT_HOLD["plus"]["G"] - SIM_DET["plus"], 2)` log points lie above the single path through the mean inputs, against `{python} points(SIM_G["plus"] - SIM_DET["plus"], 2)` before; the direction therefore rests on that scenario. As shares of spending the tilted gaps are `{python} pct(100 * TILT_ROWS['minus']['share'], 2)` and `{python} pct(100 * TILT_ROWS['plus']['share'], 2)` (@tbl-scenarios), both below the OBR long-term path's `{python} pct(SHARE['wedge'][0], 2)`: on the tilted paths the scenarios would fall below the OBR long-term path, and the gap left to DWP's figure (@sec-dwp) would widen. The diagnostic rests on few effective paths and is outside the registered rule.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-scenarios
#| tbl-cap: "Reduction in State Pension spending under the adjusted Triple Lock relative to the triple lock, £ billion, UK, cash terms; in the final year also as a share of basic and new State Pension spending under the triple lock and as the log gap G between the rules, log points. The OBR central and long-term paths are single microsimulation runs, on which G = −ln(1 − share). The earnings scenarios are stratified estimates over the same `{python} N_DRAWS` simulated paths, each run through the microsimulation, ± the 95% Monte Carlo error; their G is the average of G over the paths (rule arithmetic), slightly above −ln(1 − share) of the average share because the logarithm is convex. The last two rows reweight the scenarios' paths to the realised share of floor years (@sec-budget): a diagnostic, outside the registered rule, with the saving at each scenario's own spending base; the lower-earnings row also raises mean earnings. A scenario envelope, not a probability interval."
def _cell(v, e, d=1):
    return num(v, d) if e is None else f"{num(v, d)} ± {num(e, d)}"
NAMES = {"central": "OBR central path", "wedge": "OBR long-term path (triple lock at the OBR's long-term rate from April 2032)"}
body = []
for s in D.scenarios([MID, FINAL]):
    name = NAMES.get(s["key"], s["name"] + f", average of {N_DRAWS} paths")
    v = s["values"]
    sh, she = SHARE[s["key"]]
    g_cell = num(100 * GAP[s["key"]], 2) if s["key"] in ("central", "wedge") else \
        _cell(100 * SIM_G[s["key"]], 100 * SIM_GE[s["key"]], 2)
    body.append([name] + [c for y in (MID, FINAL) for c in (_cell(v[y][0], v[y][2]), _cell(v[y][1], v[y][3]))]
                + [_cell(sh, she, 2), g_cell])
for k, label in (("minus", f"Earnings {MINUS_SHIFT}, reweighted (diagnostic)"),
                 ("plus", f"Earnings +{SHIFT}, reweighted, mean earnings held (diagnostic)")):
    tr = TILT_ROWS[k]
    body.append([label, "–", "–", num(tr["share"] * BASE_SC[k], 1), "–", num(100 * tr["share"], 2),
                 num(100 * tr["G"], 2)])
display(Markdown(md_table(["Scenario", f"{fy(MID)}: Gross", f"{fy(MID)}: Net", f"{fy(FINAL)}: Gross",
                           f"{fy(FINAL)}: Net", f"{fy(FINAL)}: Share of spending (%)", f"{fy(FINAL)}: G"],
                          body, "lrrrrrr")))
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-scenarios
#| fig-cap: "The saving opens after the switch and grows through the decade on the simulated scenarios and the OBR long-term path, while it stays small on the OBR central path. Gross saving in each fiscal year from the switch on the four scenarios, £ billion; the shaded bands are ± the 95% Monte Carlo error on the earnings scenarios' averages."
F.scenario_years();
```

### The OBR central path {#sec-paths}

```{python}
crows = D.path_rows(central)
floor_years = [r["year"] for r in crows if r["tl_source"] == "floor"]
after = [r for r in crows if r["year"] >= SWITCH]
first_earn = next(r for r in after if r["tl_source"] == "earnings")
differ = [r for r in crows if D.differs(r)]
p50, p90, rnd = D.path("monthly_p50"), D.path("monthly_p90"), D.path("random")
```

The OBR central path is one smooth path. The floor sets the triple lock in April `{python} listing(floor_years)`; from April `{python} first_earn["year"]` earnings lead every year (@fig-central). The two rules differ in `{python} words(len(differ))` year`{python} "" if len(differ) == 1 else "s"`, April `{python} listing([r["year"] for r in differ])`: after the floor years the adjusted Triple Lock rises only by the floor, or by what brings it back to its earnings path, while the triple lock rises with earnings from the higher level. By `{python} fy(FINAL)` the full new State Pension is `{python} gbp(52 * c_final["tl_weekly"])` a year under the triple lock and `{python} gbp(52 * c_final["bp_weekly"])` under the adjusted rule, and the saving is `{python} bn(c_g, 1)` (`{python} bn(c_n, 1)` net). The OBR finds the same for its forecast period: "`{python} obr_medium`" [@obr_efo2026oct, para. 3.50, footnote 17].
