```{python}
#| label: fig-central
#| fig-cap: "On the OBR central path the floor sets the early rises, and the adjusted Triple Lock differs from the triple lock in one April, 2032; the gap then persists. Left: the inputs behind each April's rise, shown at the April they set. Centre: the April rise under each rule; the dotted line marks the switch. Right: how far the adjusted rule's full new State Pension sits below the triple lock's, in per cent; a gap this small is close to the log gap G between the rules in log points."
F.path_view("central");
```

### The mechanism on simulated paths {#sec-simpaths}

```{python}
SEL = {s["quantile"]: s for s in D.TRAJ["models"]["boot"]["selections"]}
QG = D.TRAJ["models"]["boot"]["gap_gbp_week"]
rnd_gap = D.row(rnd, FINAL)["tl_weekly"] - D.row(rnd, FINAL)["bp_weekly"]
rnd_q = max(int(k[1:]) for k, v in QG.items() if v <= rnd_gap)
rnd_q_hi = min(int(k[1:]) for k, v in QG.items() if v > rnd_gap)
LEADS = {pid: D.path_leads(pid) for pid in ("central", "wedge", "random", "monthly_p50", "monthly_p90")}
```

We run three simulated paths through the microsimulation: one drawn at random, and two picked near given percentiles of the gap between the rules in `{python} fy(FINAL)` among the `{python} N_POP` draws, one at the `{python} ordinal(100 * SEL[0.5]["cdf_position"])` percentile and one at the `{python} ordinal(100 * SEL[0.9]["cdf_position"])`. The random path's gap, `{python} gbp(52 * rnd_gap)` a year, lies between the `{python} ordinal(rnd_q)` and `{python} ordinal(rnd_q_hi)` percentiles. Each is one path the model makes, not a forecast, and carries no probability weight. @fig-gaps shows how far apart the two rules end on each, beside the two OBR scenarios. @tbl-paths gives, for each path, the saving, the changes of lead, the Aprils with earnings growth below the floor and the last April in which prices or the floor led. It also counts the Aprils in which the adjusted rule rises by less than earnings, which the change to section 150A would have to allow (@sec-two-rules), and gives the share of the triple lock's excess over earnings, $G_t/y_t$, that the adjusted rule removes. That share is all of the excess on the two OBR paths, on which earnings lead in every April after the last price- or floor-led one in April `{python} D.last_price_led('central')`. It is less on simulated paths whose last price- or floor-led years come late, so that earnings-led years have not yet worked off their excess by `{python} fy(FINAL)`: the random path's last such April is `{python} D.last_price_led('random')` and the path near the median gap's `{python} D.last_price_led('monthly_p50')`. Most of a path's saving comes from a few years of high inflation or weak earnings followed by years in which earnings lead, after which the gap stays. The count of changes of lead does not order the savings, because the increment depends on the size of each lead as well as its timing: the path near the 90th percentile has fewer changes of lead than the path near the median, but a longer run of earnings-led years after its price-led ones. The random path's pension is higher under both rules because it draws higher CPI and earnings growth than the OBR's forecast, which also raises the spending base behind its saving.

```{python}
#| label: fig-gaps
#| fig-cap: "On simulated paths the gap opens in a few steps and then persists. How far the adjusted Triple Lock's full new State Pension ends below the triple lock's on each path run through the microsimulation, £ a year."
F.gaps();
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-paths
#| tbl-cap: "The paths run through the microsimulation, in the final year: the full new State Pension under each rule, the saving, the average loss among households with less income than under the triple lock, and, over the Aprils from the switch to the final year (rule arithmetic), the changes of lead between earnings and the higher of CPI and the floor, the Aprils with May–July earnings growth below the floor, the last April in which the higher of CPI and the floor beat earnings, the Aprils in which the adjusted rule rose by less than earnings, and the share of the triple lock's log excess over earnings that the adjusted rule removes, G/y."
rows = []
for pid in ("central", "wedge", "random", "monthly_p50", "monthly_p90"):
    r = D.row(D.path(pid), FINAL)
    lz = LEADS[pid]
    rows.append([cap1(PATH_NAMES[pid]), gbp(52 * r["tl_weekly"]), gbp(52 * r["bp_weekly"]),
                 num(r["gross"], 2), num(r["net"], 2), gbp(r["mean_loss"]), str(lz["changes"]),
                 str(lz["below_floor"]), str(D.last_price_led(pid) or "–"), str(len(D.plan_below_earnings(pid))),
                 pct(100 * EXCESS[pid][0] / EXCESS[pid][1], 0)])
display(Markdown(md_table(["Path", "Triple lock (£ a year)", "Adjusted (£ a year)", "Gross (£bn)", "Net (£bn)",
                           "Average loss (£ a year)", "Changes of lead", "Aprils below the floor",
                           "Last April prices or floor led", "Aprils with a rise below earnings",
                           "Excess removed, G/y"], rows, "lrrrrrrrrrr")))
```

### From gross to net {#sec-net}

```{python}
acc = acc_w
dist = wedge["distribution"][str(FINAL)]
dec = dist["by_decile"]
hh = {r["hh_type"]: r for r in dist["by_hh_type"]}
pov = {p: wedge["poverty_pct"][p][str(FINAL)] for p in D.POLICIES}
low_dec = min(dec, key=lambda d: d["pct_income_change"])
EXP = "monthly_p50"  # the example pensioners' path: the OBR long-term run carries no example households
_shares = [D.borne_share(e, FINAL) for e in D.examples(D.path(EXP)).values()]
ex_lo = min(x for x in _shares if x is not None and x > 0.005)
ex_hi = max(x for x in _shares if x is not None)
ex_gain = sum(x is not None and x < -0.005 for x in _shares)
```

@tbl-account follows the gross saving on the OBR long-term path to the net saving. In `{python} fy(FINAL)` extra Pension Credit offsets `{python} bn(-acc["rows"][0][1])` of the `{python} bn(acc["gross"])` gross saving and lower income tax `{python} bn(-acc["rows"][5][1])`, leaving `{python} bn(acc["net"])` net, `{python} pct(100 * acc["net"] / acc["gross"], 0)` of the gross. The net figure counts direct taxes and benefits only, with no change in behaviour. It leaves out VAT and other indirect taxes on pensioners' lower spending, which would make it smaller. Not every offset falls on the same budget: local authorities pay council tax reduction in Great Britain (Northern Ireland has rate relief instead), part of the income tax would otherwise go to the Scottish and Welsh governments, and in Scotland the Scottish Government pays the Pension Age Winter Heating Payment in place of the Winter Fuel Payment. @tbl-account bounds the Pension Credit convention of @sec-model in one direction only. If the Pension Credit guarantee followed each rule's rise, the Pension Credit, Housing Benefit and council tax reduction offsets, `{python} bn(pc_hb_ctr, 2)` together, would vanish and could change sign, because a lower Pension Credit guarantee also lowers awards to existing claimants and moves fewer people onto the guarantee credit. The net saving on this path would then be at least about `{python} bn(pc_lb, 1)`, `{python} pct(100 * pc_lb / acc["gross"], 0)` of the gross, by an amount we do not estimate.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-account
#| tbl-cap: "From gross to net on the OBR long-term path in the final year, £ billion. Each offset is signed so the column adds up to the net saving."
# Universal Credit barely moves for pensioners; it is folded into the other taxes and benefits.
small = [(label, v) for label, v in acc["rows"] if "Universal Credit" in label]
body = [["Gross saving (State Pension)", num(acc["gross"], 2)]]
body += [[label, num(v, 2)] for label, v in acc["rows"] if (label, v) not in small]
body.append(["Other taxes and benefits", num(acc["other"] + sum(v for _, v in small), 2)])
body.append(["**Net saving**", f'**{num(acc["net"], 2)}**'])
display(Markdown(md_table(["", f"{fy(FINAL)} (£bn)"], body)))
```

### Who has less income {#sec-incomes}

The household results run each path through PolicyEngine UK for the whole survey population, once under each rule. The model recalculates every pensioner's State Pension and, with it, their income tax, Pension Credit, Housing Benefit, council tax reduction and Winter Fuel Payment. We report them on the OBR long-term path, the largest of the single runs, and give the poverty changes on the OBR central path and the two simulated paths picked by their gap beside it. Cash and percentage changes in income scale roughly with the gap in the pension; poverty rates do not.

On the OBR long-term path households with less income under the adjusted Triple Lock than under the triple lock in `{python} fy(FINAL)` have `{python} gbp(w_loss)` a year less on average, against `{python} gbp(c_final["mean_loss"])` on the OBR central path. Single pensioners have `{python} pct(-hh["single_pensioner"]["pct_income_change"], 1)` less income than under the triple lock on average, and pensioner couples `{python} pct(-hh["pensioner_couple"]["pct_income_change"], 1)`. The share of households with at least £1 a year less income, `{python} ("about " + pct(lose_hi, 0)) if pct(lose_lo, 0) == pct(lose_hi, 0) else (pct(lose_lo, 0) + " to " + pct(lose_hi, 0))` on every path, counts the households that receive a State Pension and says nothing about the size of the effect.

@fig-deciles ranks households by equivalised household net income before housing costs under the triple lock, with each decile holding a tenth of people, and gives each decile's total change in income as a share of its total income. Relative to income, the change is largest in the `{python} ordinal(low_dec["decile"])` decile, at `{python} pct(abs(low_dec["pct_income_change"]), 2)` of income, and smaller in the lowest-income and in the higher-income deciles. The guarantee credit, which makes up a lower pension pound for pound, and the State Pension's smaller share of higher incomes both work in this direction. Four example pensioners in @sec-examples show the range: on the model path near the median gap, the share of the lower pension that reaches their income in `{python} fy(FINAL)` runs from `{python} pct(100 * ex_lo, 0)` to `{python} pct(100 * ex_hi, 0)` for those whose income falls, and `{python} words(ex_gain)` ends better off because of a threshold.

On the OBR central path, where the pension gap is small, no poverty measure changes by more than `{python} num(pov_c_max, 2)` percentage points. On the OBR long-term path pensioner poverty after housing costs is `{python} num(pov_w["pensioners_absolute_ahc"], 2)` points higher against the fixed line and `{python} num(pov_w["pensioners_relative_ahc"], 2)` points higher against the relative one, and on the simulated path near the 90th percentile of the gap up to `{python} num(pov_p90_max, 2)` points higher (@tbl-poverty). Pensioners here are people over State Pension age. The poverty changes on single paths carry no sampling margin, and we have not benchmarked the model's levels: pensioner relative poverty after housing costs under the triple lock is `{python} pct(wedge["poverty_pct"]["triple_lock"][str(D.YEARS[0])]["pensioners_relative_ahc"], 1)` in `{python} fy(D.YEARS[0])`, the first year of the runs, against DWP's modelled around `{python} dwp_pov.group(1)` for `{python} fy(int(dwp_pov.group(2)[:4]))`, also for people above State Pension age [@dwp_uprating2026]; Households Below Average Income statistics instead count people in pensioner families. Poverty among everyone changes much less, and relative poverty among everyone falls: the relative line is 60% of median income in each run, and the lower pension lowers the median, so fewer people of working age fall below the line. The fixed line is 60% of the 2024-25 median, held fixed in real terms by uprating it with each path's CPI, so it differs between paths; it also differs from the official absolute measure in Households Below Average Income statistics, which DWP anchors in 2010-11. Pension Credit makes up much of a lower pension for pensioners on the guarantee credit, but not for those just above it.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-poverty
#| tbl-cap: "Poverty after housing costs in the final year: share of people in households below the line, %, and the change under the adjusted Triple Lock, percentage points. Levels are for the OBR long-term path only. Fixed line: below 60% of the 2024-25 median, uprated by each path's CPI, so the line differs between paths. Relative: below 60% of the median in the same run."
PM = [("pensioners_absolute_ahc", "Pensioners, fixed line"), ("pensioners_relative_ahc", "Pensioners, relative"),
      ("everyone_absolute_ahc", "Everyone, fixed line"), ("everyone_relative_ahc", "Everyone, relative")]
body = [[label, num(pov["triple_lock"][k], 2), num(pov["burnham_2030"][k], 2)]
        + [num(pov_change(D.path(pid), k), 2) for pid in PATHS_HH] for k, label in PM]
display(Markdown(md_table(["Measure", "Triple lock (%)", "Adjusted (%)", "Change, OBR central (points)",
                           "Change, OBR long term (points)", "Change, median-gap path (points)",
                           "Change, 90th-percentile path (points)"], body)))
```

## Comparison with official costings {#sec-dwp}

```{python}
bmk = {b["id"]: b for b in D.R["benchmarks"]}
frs25 = re.search(r"£[\d.]+ billion", bmk["obr_frs_2025"]["figure_text"]).group(0)
cov = D.R["coverage"]
cov_rows = {r["key"]: r for r in cov["rows"]}
sp_ratio = cov_rows["state_pension_bn"]["primary_gb_over_dwp"]
flat_ratio = cov_rows["flat_rate_bn"]["primary_gb_over_dwp"]
DEFL = D.price_level(2025, FINAL)  # 2025-26 prices: the central path's CPI from 2025 to the final year
obr_replay_avg = re.search(r"([\d.]+) per cent lower", bmk["obr_efo_2026_historical_replay"]["figure_text"]).group(1)
dwp_caution = re.sub(r"\s+", " ", re.search(r"should not be used to then derive further point estimates for savings in an "
                                           r"individual year", DWP_TEXT).group(0))
# DWP's base-scaled residual: its cash figure, which covers ±£0.5bn of rounding, less our Great Britain savings scaled
# between the two coverage ratios.
DWP_LO, DWP_HI = float(dwp_nominal) - 0.5, float(dwp_nominal) + 0.5
res_lo = DWP_LO - gb["plus"] / flat_ratio
res_hi = DWP_HI - gb["minus"] / sp_ratio
res_w_lo, res_w_hi = DWP_LO - gb["wedge"] / flat_ratio, DWP_HI - gb["wedge"] / sp_ratio
# The OBR long-term path with the premium in full from April 2031 (rule arithmetic), in Great Britain at DWP's base.
gb_share = gb["wedge"] / w_g  # Great Britain's share of the UK saving on this path
wf_gb_lo, wf_gb_hi = WF_GROSS * gb_share / sp_ratio, WF_GROSS * gb_share / flat_ratio
# The replay's triple-lock excess over its published earnings path in cash, 2026-27: its basic and new State Pension
# spending (the replay's gross saving over its level gap) times one less the inverse of the level ratio.
B_2026 = past_saving["gross"] / (hw_first["gap_pct"] / 100)
TL_EXCESS_2026 = (1 - 1 / (1 + above_earn / 100)) * B_2026
new_sp_share = (lambda s: sum(v["new_recipients_m"] for v in s.values()) / sum(v["recipients_m"] for v in s.values()))(
    D.R["coverage"]["state_pension_by_age"]["primary"][str(FINAL)])
```

DWP costs the adjusted Triple Lock at £`{python} dwp_nominal`bn in `{python} fy(FINAL)` in cash terms [@dwp_uprating2026], and the Budget repeats the figure (@sec-intro). It is direct spending for Great Britain, rounded to the nearest billion, so it covers £`{python} num(DWP_LO, 1)`bn to £`{python} num(DWP_HI, 1)`bn, and it leaves out tax and debt interest. DWP's method note says that "`{python} dwp_model`" and that "`{python} dwp_cpi`" [@dwp_uprating2026]; its model is a dynamic microsimulation model of the kind @li2013 review. The government has said, in answer to a parliamentary question, that DWP's analysis did not use single-year earnings or prices growth assumptions [@hl3774]. That makes it closer in kind to the OBR's average-rate convention than to a simulated path, so we infer that the OBR long-term path is the closest of our scenarios in method. The Budget publishes the trajectory behind the figure only as a chart of State Pension spending as a share of GDP under each rule [@budget2026, Box 5.A], which we read from its vector file to about `{python} num(D.CHART_PRECISION, 2)` points of GDP, a reading the Budget does not tabulate (the paper's repository holds the readings, the method and the file's provenance, under data/benchmarks). On our reading, the adjusted rule's spending is `{python} pct(100 * CH[MID], 1)` below the triple lock's in `{python} fy(MID)` and `{python} pct(100 * CH[FINAL], 1)` below in `{python} fy(FINAL)`, against `{python} pct(SHARE_MID['wedge'][0], 2)` and `{python} pct(SHARE['wedge'][0], 2)` on our OBR long-term path and at most `{python} pct(max(SHARE['minus'][0], SHARE['plus'][0]), 2)` in `{python} fy(FINAL)` on the scenarios, and its two lines first part in `{python} fy(CH_FIRST)`, as the rules can first differ in April `{python} SWITCH + 1` here. The government's own path therefore saves a larger share of spending than any of our scenarios.

Our nearest figures are the gross savings in Great Britain: `{python} bn(gb["central"], 1)` on the OBR central path, `{python} bn(gb["wedge"], 1)` on the OBR long-term path, and `{python} bn(gb["minus"], 1)` and `{python} bn(gb["plus"], 1)` on the two earnings scenarios. The population also differs. DWP projects deaths, migration and State Pension entitlements, while we keep today's survey records and rake their weights to the ONS's projected growth by age and sex (@sec-population). Our survey's spending on the basic and new State Pension, the base the saving scales with, is `{python} pct(100 * flat_ratio, 0)` of DWP's forecast for `{python} fy(cov["year"])` (@tbl-coverage), but that ratio compares our Great Britain base with a DWP base that includes State Pensions paid abroad, which DWP's Great Britain costing leaves out. On total State Pension excluding payments abroad our survey matches `{python} pct(100 * sp_ratio, 0)` of DWP's forecast, so the like-for-like ratio for the basic and new State Pension lies between `{python} num(flat_ratio, 2)` and about `{python} num(sp_ratio, 2)`. Since the gross saving is close to $(1 - e^{-G_t})B^{\mathrm{TL}}_t$, scaling our base to DWP's raises the Great Britain figures in proportion, to `{python} bn(gb["wedge"] / sp_ratio, 1)` to `{python} bn(gb["wedge"] / flat_ratio, 1)` on the OBR long-term path. Allowing for DWP's rounding, that leaves `{python} bn(res_w_lo, 1)` to `{python} bn(res_w_hi, 1)` of DWP's figure, `{python} pct(100 * res_w_lo / float(dwp_nominal), 0)` to `{python} pct(100 * res_w_hi / float(dwp_nominal), 0)` of it (`{python} pct(100 * res_lo / float(dwp_nominal), 0)` to `{python} pct(100 * res_hi / float(dwp_nominal), 0)` on the scenarios).

Most of that residual is in the share of spending saved, not in the base. By the bound of @sec-formal, a saving of `{python} pct(100 * CH[FINAL], 1)` of spending needs a triple-lock excess of at least `{python} points(CH_G, 2)` log points by `{python} fy(FINAL)`, about `{python} points(CH_PER, 2)` a year over the Aprils from `{python} CH_FIRST`, the first in which the chart's lines part, while the premium we apply phases in from April `{python} D.OBR_LT_FROM`. Paying the premium in full from April `{python} SWITCH + 1`, in rule arithmetic with caseloads held, raises the gap on the OBR long-term path to `{python} points(WF['G'], 2)` log points, a share of `{python} pct(100 * WF_SHARE, 1)`, and the Great Britain saving at DWP's base to `{python} bn(wf_gb_lo, 1)` to `{python} bn(wf_gb_hi, 1)`, so the start date of the premium accounts for most of the residual. Other candidate sources, none of which we test, are DWP's own uprating path, later cohorts' larger new State Pension entitlements, which our base may understate (`{python} pct(100 * new_sp_share, 0)` of recipients in `{python} fy(FINAL)` in the raked survey are on the new State Pension, with entitlements carried forward from today's pensioners), and State Pension age. Both of the chart's lines fall as a share of GDP from `{python} fy(CH_DIPS[1][0])` to `{python} fy(CH_DIPS[1][1])`, as they do from `{python} fy(CH_DIPS[0][0])` to `{python} fy(CH_DIPS[0][1])` while State Pension age rises to `{python} SPA_67`; our runs keep State Pension age on the law's timetable, which reaches `{python} SPA_68` only from `{python} SPA_68_FROM` [@pa2007]. The Budget does not say why its lines fall, so this is a check, not a finding.

We cannot compare DWP's £`{python} dwp_real`bn in 2025-26 prices more closely, because DWP does not state its deflator. DWP adds that its savings "`{python} dwp_caution`", and its saving keeps growing, to £`{python} dwp_later`bn in `{python} fy(dwp_later_year)`; our horizon ends in `{python} fy(FINAL)`.

The OBR's own figures measure related but different things. Its footnote on the medium-term forecast matches our OBR central path, on which the adjusted rule rises by `{python} FLOOR` in April `{python} SWITCH` and `{python} SWITCH + 1` [@obr_efo2026oct, para. 3.50, footnote 17]. Its replay of 1990–2025, with the anchor set in 1990, puts payments under the adjusted rule `{python} num(OBR_LO, 1)`% lower on average than under the triple lock and `{python} num(OBR_HI, 1)`% higher than under earnings uprating [@obr_efo2026oct, para. 3.51], so on that replay the adjusted rule removes about `{python} pct(100 * OBR_REPLAY_SHARE, 0)` of the triple lock's average log excess over earnings; the same average gap on our replay, which starts in April `{python} hw_first["first"]`, is `{python} pct(avg_gap, 1)` (@sec-past). Its provisional long-term estimate, debt about `{python} num(DEBT_TL, 0)`% of GDP lower than under the triple lock and about `{python} num(DEBT_E, 0)`% higher than under earnings uprating in 2075-76 [@obr_efo2026oct, para. 3.52], corresponds to about `{python} pct(100 * OBR_DEBT_SHARE, 0)`. These are averages over years and shares of debt, not of the pension's level in one year, so they do not compare directly with our `{python} pct(100 * G_HIST / Y_HIST, 0)` on the replay and `{python} pct(100 * SIM_G["minus"] / SIM_Y["minus"], 0)` and `{python} pct(100 * SIM_G["plus"] / SIM_Y["plus"], 0)` on the scenarios. Its estimate that the triple lock will have added `{python} frs25` a year by 2029-30 compares the triple lock with earnings uprating since 2011 [@obr_frs2025]. The like-for-like figure on our replay is the triple lock's excess over its earnings path in `{python} fy(LAST_HIST)`, `{python} pct(above_earn, 1)`, about `{python} bn(TL_EXCESS_2026, 0)` of basic and new State Pension spending, of which the adjusted rule started in April `{python} hw_first["first"]` would remove `{python} bn(past_saving["gross"], 1)`.

DWP also projects pensioner relative poverty after housing costs under the adjusted Triple Lock falling from around `{python} dwp_pov.group(1)` to around `{python} dwp_pov.group(3)` by `{python} dwp_pov.group(4)`-`{python} dwp_pov.group(5)[-2:]`, against a poverty line projected forward with earnings. Our poverty rates (@sec-incomes) are for `{python} fy(FINAL)`, use a line set each year from the simulated incomes, and compare the adjusted Triple Lock with the triple lock rather than with today, so they answer a different question.

## Discussion {#sec-discussion}

Two points bear on how analysts cost max-of-indices rules. First, the decomposition $y_t = x_t + G_t$ of @sec-formal says which part of the triple lock's excess over earnings an earnings-anchored rule removes. Path by path, it removes all of it when enough earnings-led years follow price- or floor-led ones, as on both OBR paths by construction, and none of an excess that arrives at the end of the horizon. On past inputs (@sec-past) and on average over the two scenarios, whose model overstates how often the lead changes, it removes part of the excess; on the scenarios most of the average gap comes from year-to-year variation rather than from the paths' mean (@sec-budget). The OBR's long-term premium is a reduced-form allowance for the same effect, which is why the scenario built on it bounds the share saved only within that convention.

Second, the failed condition points towards overstatement (@sec-test). A floor year adds to the gap only when earnings lead later, and larger earnings leads use up the excess faster, so fewer floor years with stronger earnings could open the gap faster, and the direction of the bias is not obvious beforehand. The reweighting diagnostic of @sec-budget settles it for the scenario in which mean earnings can be held fixed. That diagnostic is not an estimate, and a model that passed the test could still differ from it. The second model does not corroborate that direction (@sec-c4).

The paper gives no probability distribution because both registered models failed; the forecast record explains why a pass would not have been enough. Had the second model passed, the analysis plan left it to the second author to decide whether its distribution could replace the scenarios, and the test could not have seen the drift of its centre in years five to `{python} words(C4_AHEAD)` (@sec-c4). The OBR's record holds `{python} words(n_c4)` yearly forecasts with four years of statutory outturns, and their windows overlap, covering `{python} words(len(C4_SPAN))` years of inputs, `{python} C4_SPAN[0]` to `{python} C4_SPAN[-1]`. The saving in `{python} fy(FINAL)` depends on inputs up to `{python} words(C4_AHEAD)` years ahead, and no forecast in the record runs that far, so any model of the later years must assume how errors at four years carry on, and no complete forecast can test that assumption. Suppose the OBR's long-term assumptions of the time extended the four scored years of each forecast made in `{python} C4_EXT[0]` to `{python} C4_EXT[-1]` by `{python} words(C4_AHEAD - 4)` more. Those `{python} words(C4_AHEAD)`-year windows would overlap, and `{python} words(len(C4_SPAN))` years of outturns hold at most `{python} words(len(C4_SPAN) // C4_AHEAD)` independent window of that length. The second model carries forward the four-year-ahead errors of past target years, and the errors for `{python} C4_LATE[0]` to `{python} C4_LATE[-1]`, when May–July earnings growth rebounded after furlough and inflation peaked, enter the later years of most of its paths (@sec-c4). For independent, normal yearly differences the expected gap rises with their spread (@sec-formal), and the second model's mean share falls roughly in proportion when its errors are scaled down (@sec-c4), so its distribution reports which past years it replays. Neither registered model passed, a third would face the same `{python} words(n_c4)` forecasts, and the analysis plan leaves estimates to the forward rule's test on outcomes not yet observed (@sec-test).

The results bear on any rule that pays the highest of several indices. Where the yearly differences are persistent, or rarely change lead, an earnings anchor removes almost all of a smooth premium; where the lead changes often and price-led years come late, it removes much less, because at any date the adjusted rule still carries part of the excess. A fiscal council that enters such a rule in its long-term projections as a smooth premium over earnings therefore attributes all of the excess to the ratchet, and the replay (@sec-past) suggests that is too much. Proposition 2 gives a way to represent the rule with little more than the mean and variance of the yearly differences: on the replay's inputs it gives an expected gap of `{python} pct(100 * SP_H[0] / SP_H[1], 0)` of the expected excess, against the `{python} pct(100 * G_HIST / Y_HIST, 0)` realised.

## Conclusion {#sec-conclusion}

The adjusted Triple Lock keeps the triple lock's protection against prices and its `{python} FLOOR` floor, but lets the pension fall back to its April `{python} SWITCH - 1` value relative to earnings after years in which prices or the floor beat earnings. Its saving therefore depends on how often the lead passes from prices or the floor to earnings, not only on their expected growth: it grows only in earnings-led years that follow a price- or floor-led one. Replayed from April `{python} hw_first["first"]` on today's figures, it would remove `{python} pct(100 * G_HIST / Y_HIST, 0)` of the triple lock's excess and leave the pension `{python} pct(hw_first["gap_pct"], 1)` below the triple lock in `{python} fy(LAST_HIST)`. For the UK in `{python} fy(FINAL)`, on the OBR's smooth central path it lowers State Pension spending by `{python} bn(c_g, 1)`; with the OBR's long-term premium applied to the triple lock only, by `{python} bn(w_g, 1)`, or `{python} pct(SHARE['wedge'][0], 2)` of spending, a share that is an upper bound within that convention only; and on average over simulated paths with earnings growth `{python} SHIFT` points lower or higher by `{python} bn(lo_g, 1)` or `{python} bn(hi_g, 1)`, `{python} bn(lo_n, 1)` or `{python} bn(hi_n, 1)` after tax and benefits respond. These are scenarios, not a range with probabilities attached: our model of prices and earnings failed a registered test on past forecasts by overstating how often earnings growth falls below the floor, so the paper gives no expected value, and reweighting the higher-earnings paths to the realised frequency, holding mean earnings fixed, lowers their gap. The government's own trajectory saves `{python} pct(100 * CH[FINAL], 1)` of spending in `{python} fy(FINAL)`, more than any of our scenarios. Scaled to DWP's population base, the OBR long-term path, the closest of them in method, leaves `{python} pct(100 * res_w_lo / float(dwp_nominal), 0)` to `{python} pct(100 * res_w_hi / float(dwp_nominal), 0)` of DWP's £`{python} dwp_nominal`bn unexplained (`{python} pct(100 * res_lo / float(dwp_nominal), 0)` to `{python} pct(100 * res_hi / float(dwp_nominal), 0)` on the scenarios), most of which, in rule arithmetic, a start of the OBR's premium in April `{python} SWITCH + 1` would account for; we cannot decompose it further without DWP's path.

The loss falls on households that receive a State Pension, with Pension Credit and income tax making up part of it: on the OBR long-term path the government keeps `{python} bn(acc_w["net"], 1)` of the gross saving, `{python} pct(100 * acc_w["net"] / acc_w["gross"], 0)`, and at least about `{python} bn(pc_lb, 1)` (`{python} pct(100 * pc_lb / acc_w["gross"], 0)`) if the Pension Credit guarantee followed each rule's rise. On that path pensioner poverty after housing costs rises by `{python} num(pov_w["pensioners_absolute_ahc"], 2)` percentage points against the fixed line and `{python} num(pov_w["pensioners_relative_ahc"], 2)` against the relative one. The rule would also require a change to the statutory earnings link. For any uprating rule that takes the highest of several indices, the cost of removing the ratchet depends on how the indices vary from year to year, and a test of the model of that variation decides what we can report: here, scenarios, until the forward rule of @sec-test can first report.

The analysis has limits. It gives no expected value, and the direction of the failed condition's effect on the scenario averages rests on a diagnostic, not an estimate. A second model of the inputs, built on the OBR's forecast errors, also failed its registered test. Beyond four years ahead the only check is one realised path since 2011, which the baseline model met and the second model could not be scored on, so the paper gives no probability distribution of the saving. The simulated paths rest on one model of monthly prices and earnings, centred on the OBR's forecasts, with no periods of changing volatility, and they change lead more often than the records since 2011 and since 1989, a rate we have not tested against the fitting window. The survey's records keep their ages and only their weights follow the ONS's projected growth by age and sex, its basic and new State Pension spending in Great Britain is `{python} pct(100 * flat_ratio, 0)` to `{python} pct(100 * sp_ratio, 0)` of DWP's forecast, depending on how payments abroad are treated, and we have not checked projected spending in `{python} fy(FINAL)` against the OBR's long-term projection. Our runs hold behaviour fixed, Housing Benefit and council tax reduction respond only for households already receiving them, and the runs leave out indirect taxes, so the net figures count direct taxes and benefits only.

## Appendix: proofs {#sec-proof .appendix}

*The recursions.* From the level equations, $y_t - y_{t-1} = \ln(1 + \max(m_t, e_t)) - \ln(1 + e_t) = \max(d_t, 0)$, and $x_t = \ln \max\bigl((L_{t-1}/A_{t-1})(1 + m_t)/(1 + e_t),\, 1\bigr) = \max(x_{t-1} + d_t, 0)$. Hence $\Delta G_t = \max(d_t, 0) - \max(d_t, -x_{t-1})$, which is zero when $d_t \ge 0$ and $\min(-d_t, x_{t-1})$ when $d_t < 0$; since $x_{t-1} \ge 0$ this is $\min(\max(-d_t, 0), x_{t-1}) \ge 0$. Summing, the reflected walk has the standard solution of a Lindley recursion, $x_t = D_t - \min_{T_0 \le s \le t} D_s$ [@asmussen2003], and $y_t = \sum_s \max(d_s, 0)$, which gives the closed form for $G_t$. The upper bounds follow from $x_t \ge 0$ and from $\min_s D_s \le D_{T_0} = 0$.

*Proposition 1.* If $\Delta G_r > 0$ then $d_r < 0$ and $x_{r-1} > 0$, and $x_{r-1} > 0$ requires some $s < r$ with $d_s > 0$, since $x$ starts at zero and rises only when $d > 0$. Conversely, take $s$ with $d_s > 0$ and the first $r > s$ with $d_r < 0$; between them every $d \ge 0$, so $x_{r-1} \ge x_s \ge d_s > 0$ and $\Delta G_r > 0$. So $G_t > 0$ exactly when such a pair $s < r \le t$ exists. If $d_s \le 0$ in every year, $x$ stays at zero and $G_t = y_t = 0$; if $d_s \ge 0$ in every year, no increment is positive and $G_t = 0$.

*Proposition 2.* Write $n$ for the number of rises and number the differences $d_1, \dots, d_n$, with $D_k = d_1 + \dots + d_k$ and $D_0 = 0$. The solution of the Lindley recursion is $x_n = D_n - \min_{0 \le s \le n} D_s = \max_{0 \le s \le n} (D_n - D_s)$, and $D_n - D_s$ is the sum of the last $n - s$ differences. Under independence with a common distribution, $(d_1, \dots, d_n)$ has the same law as $(d_n, \dots, d_1)$, so $x_n$ has the law of the running maximum $\max_{0 \le k \le n} D_k$, whose expectation is $\sum_{k=1}^{n} \mathrm{E}[(D_k)^{+}]/k$ by Spitzer's identity [@spitzer1956]. With $\mathrm{E}[y_n] = n\,\mathrm{E}[d^{+}]$ this gives the expression for $\mathrm{E}[G_n]$. If $d \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)$ then $D_k \sim N(k\mu, k\sigma^2)$, and for $X \sim N(m, s^2)$, $\mathrm{E}[X^{+}] = m\,\Phi(m/s) + s\,\varphi(m/s)$, whose derivative in $s$ is $\varphi(m/s)$. Hence
$$\frac{\partial\, \mathrm{E}[G_n]}{\partial \sigma} = \sum_{k=1}^{n} \Bigl(\varphi(\mu/\sigma) - \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{k}}\,\varphi(\sqrt{k}\,\mu/\sigma)\Bigr) \ge 0,$$
since $\varphi(\sqrt{k}\,a) \le \varphi(a)$ and $1/\sqrt{k} \le 1$ for $k \ge 1$. At $\sigma = 0$ each term of $\mathrm{E}[G_n]$ is $\mu^{+} - (k\mu)^{+}/k = 0$.

## Appendix: further results {#sec-appendix .appendix}

This appendix gives the data against DWP's benefit expenditure and caseload forecasts [@dwp_bect2026] (@tbl-coverage), the scores of each version of the model of prices and earnings in the test on past forecasts (@tbl-screen and @tbl-screen-bias), and the record of the test's rules. @sec-examples runs four example pensioners.

We recorded the second rule of the test in a dated section of the analysis plan, committed on its own on `{python} V2["c2_registered"]`, before we computed any score under it. The forward rule gives its first verdict after `{python} words(D.C3_YEARS)` years of outcomes. On simulated outcomes a correct model passes that test `{python} pct(100 * D.c3_pass_rate("model is right", 4), 1)` of the time after four years, `{python} pct(100 * D.c3_pass_rate("model is right", 8), 1)` after eight and `{python} pct(100 * D.c3_pass_rate("model is right", 12), 1)` after twelve. A model that states double the true rate of earnings growth below the floor passes `{python} pct(100 * D.c3_pass_rate("true floor rate is 1/2 of the model's", 4), 1)`, `{python} pct(100 * D.c3_pass_rate("true floor rate is 1/2 of the model's", 8), 1)` and `{python} pct(100 * D.c3_pass_rate("true floor rate is 1/2 of the model's", 12), 1)`. Four years of outcomes cannot tell the two apart.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-coverage
#| tbl-cap: "Our data against DWP's Spring Forecast 2026, Great Britain. Microcosm is the dataset every result uses; the Enhanced FRS is a check only. Claims are counted in benefit units. (a) DWP's figure includes payments abroad, which ours do not. (b) Excludes Universal Credit housing costs."
COV_LABELS = {
    "state_pension_bn": "State Pension, excluding payments abroad (£bn)",
    "flat_rate_bn": "Basic and new State Pension (a) (£bn)",
    "state_pension_recipients_m": "State Pension recipients (m)",
    "pension_credit_bn": "Pension Credit (£bn)",
    "pension_credit_claims_m": "Pension Credit claims (m)",
    "housing_benefit_bn": "Housing Benefit, all ages (b) (£bn)",
    "housing_benefit_pension_age_bn": "Housing Benefit, pension age (£bn)",
    "housing_benefit_pension_age_claims_m": "Housing Benefit claims, pension age (m)",
}
body = []
for r in cov["rows"]:
    d = 2 if r["key"].endswith("_m") else 1
    body.append([COV_LABELS.get(r["key"], r["label"]), num(r["dwp"], d),
                 num(r["primary_gb"], d), pct(100 * r["primary_gb_over_dwp"], 0),
                 num(r["sensitivity_gb"], d), pct(100 * r["sensitivity_gb_over_dwp"], 0)])
display(Markdown(md_table([fy(cov["year"]), "DWP", "Microcosm: Value", "Microcosm: % of DWP",
                           f"Enhanced FRS {V2['efrs']}: Value", f"Enhanced FRS {V2['efrs']}: % of DWP"], body)))
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-screen
#| tbl-cap: "The test on past forecasts, with April 2022 scored as in law: coverage, accuracy scores and verdict. Seven forecasts: one a year, March 2016 to March 2022; thirteen forecasts: June 2010 to March 2022. Yearly: share of yearly gaps inside each version's central 80% band; four-year: four-year gaps inside it; plausible range: the 95% Wilson interval for four-year coverage on the seven-forecast test, which must include 80%; it is the same for every version with the same number of hits. Score ratio: the largest ratio of the version's accuracy scores to the baseline model's."
SCORES = ("gap_crps", "switch_crps", "floor_crps", "energy", "variogram")
sc_all = D.C2["scores"]
body = []
for form, verdict in forms.items():
    cells = []
    for test in ("A", "B"):
        r = sc_all[test]["suspended"][form]
        cells += [pct(100 * r["annual_gap_coverage"]["mean"], 0), f'{r["terminal_coverage"]["hits"]} of {r["terminal_scored_origins"]}']
    lo_w, hi_w = sc_all["A"]["suspended"][form]["terminal_coverage"]["wilson95_independent"]
    worst = max(sc_all[t]["suspended"][form][k]["mean"] / sc_all[t]["suspended"][D.PRIMARY_FORM][k]["mean"]
                for t in ("A", "B") for k in SCORES)
    body.append([D.FORM_NAMES.get(form, form), *cells, f"{pct(100 * lo_w, 0)} to {pct(100 * hi_w, 0)}",
                 num(worst, 2), "Pass" if verdict["passes"] else "Fail"])
display(Markdown(md_table(["Version", "Seven forecasts: Yearly", "Seven forecasts: Four-year",
                           "Thirteen forecasts: Yearly", "Thirteen forecasts: Four-year", "Plausible range",
                           "Score ratio", "Verdict"], body, "lrrrrrrl")))
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-screen-bias
#| tbl-cap: "The test on past forecasts, continued: the bias conditions on the seven-forecast test, with April 2022 scored as in law, and the past-years check. Floor years: the share of years with earnings growth below the floor that the version expected (realised: `{python} pct(100 * A['realised_floor_frequency']['mean'], 1)`); floor bias is the difference (limit `{python} num(D.SCREEN_RULE['floor_bias'], 2)`). Lead changes: expected per four-year window (realised: `{python} num(A['realised_switches']['mean'], 2)`); lead bias is the difference (limit `{python} num(D.SCREEN_RULE['switch_bias'], 1)`). Gap bias: average error in earnings minus CPI, points (limit `{python} num(D.SCREEN_RULE['gap_bias'], 1)`). Every bias is the version's expectation less the realised value. Past years: the percentile of the realised gap since 2011 among the version's paths (limits in @tbl-rule)."
body = []
for form in forms:
    r = sc_all["A"]["suspended"][form]
    body.append([D.FORM_NAMES.get(form, form), pct(100 * r["predicted_floor_frequency"]["mean"], 1),
                 num(r["floor_bias"]["mean"], 3), num(r["predicted_switches"]["mean"], 2),
                 num(r["switch_bias"]["mean"], 2), num(r["gap_bias_pp"]["mean"], 2),
                 ordinal(D.C2["past_years"][form]["suspended"]["realised_percentile"])])
display(Markdown(md_table(["Version", "Floor years (%)", "Floor bias", "Lead changes", "Lead bias", "Gap bias",
                           "Past years"], body, "lrrrrrr")))
```

The analysis plan requires this appendix because the second model of @sec-test failed its test. Every figure here is the output of a model that failed its registered test and is not a probability statement: the paper attaches no likelihood to any of them, takes none as an estimate and converts none to cash. Years five to twelve of each path are untested, because no forecast in the record runs that far and no scored window reaches them. The model draws `{python} count(D.C4_PATHS)` paths of September CPI and May–July earnings growth around the OBR central path, for the Aprils `{python} c4_first_april` to `{python} c4_last_april`, from all `{python} words(n_c4)` forecasts, and applies both rules to each path in rule arithmetic (@tbl-c4-dist).`{python} " In " + fy(D.C4_YEARS[0]) + " the lower quartile is zero: on those paths no price- or floor-led April from the switch has yet been followed by an earnings-led one." if c4_none_2034 else ""` The registration fixed two tables here, the distribution (@tbl-c4-dist) and the scores (@tbl-c4-scores). We computed the seed sets, the single-score drops and the split of the variogram excess by forecast (@sec-test), the counts of error histories, the drift and the decomposition (@tbl-c4-decomp) after the verdict; none of them was registered, and no row of the decomposition is the result of a corrected model.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-c4-dist
#| tbl-cap: "The second model's distribution of the share of basic and new State Pension spending that the adjusted Triple Lock saves relative to the triple lock, %, and of the log gap G between the rules, log points, over its forward paths (rule arithmetic). The output of a model that failed its registered test, not a probability statement; mean and quartiles only."
body = []
for y in D.C4_YEARS:
    for what, label in (("share", "share of spending (%)"), ("G", "G (log points)")):
        d = D.c4_distribution(y, what)
        body.append([f"{fy(y)}: {label}", *[num(100 * d[k], 2) for k in ("mean", "p25", "median", "p75")]])
display(Markdown(md_table(["", "Mean", "Lower quartile", "Median", "Upper quartile"], body)))
```

The paths hold fewer distinct histories than their number suggests. Each path takes one past forecast's errors for its first four years and then a sequence of past four-year-ahead errors; the `{python} count(RES["n_paths"])` paths hold `{python} count(RES["distinct_histories"])` distinct histories, and the draw of the average error spreads each history's paths without adding new ones. The highest `{python} pct(RES["tail_pct"], 0)` of the share in `{python} fy(FINAL)` comes from `{python} words(top["distinct_histories"])` histories, `{python} words(top["histories_holding_half"])` of which hold half those paths, and the lowest `{python} pct(RES["tail_pct"], 0)` from `{python} words(bottom["distinct_histories"])`, `{python} words(bottom["histories_holding_half"])` of which hold half. The quartiles rest on few histories too. The paths above the upper quartile in `{python} fy(D.C4_CONC["year"])` come from `{python} count(D.C4_CONC["upper_quartile"]["distinct_histories"])` histories, `{python} words(D.C4_CONC["upper_quartile"]["histories_holding_half"])` of which hold half those paths; the five largest histories hold `{python} pct(100 * D.C4_CONC["five_largest_histories_share_of_paths"], 0)` of all paths, and `{python} pct(100 * D.C4_CONC["between_history_variance_share"], 0)` of the share's variance lies between histories. @tbl-c4-dist gives the mean and quartiles only, a reporting choice of ours. The registration also named outer percentiles and the shares of paths above several thresholds; the paper's repository holds them in `{python} (D.C4_DIR / 'rule_arithmetic.json').relative_to(D.ROOT)`, and they rest on a handful of past years.

The model's centre drifts above the OBR path after four years. Its registration describes it as centred on that path by construction, and the analysis plan records the correction. From year five each path follows the record's target years in order and restarts at random only when the record runs out, so later years draw the four-year-ahead errors for `{python} late[0]` to `{python} late[-1]` more often than uniform sampling would: on `{python} pct(100 * min(late_w), 0)` to `{python} pct(100 * max(late_w), 0)` of the draws in each year, against `{python} pct(100 * DR["uniform_weight_on_late_targets"], 0)`. Those errors are positive, so the mean error in the statutory inputs rises from `{python} num(ex_c[first_drift], 2)` points for CPI and `{python} num(ex_e[first_drift], 2)` for earnings in the inputs for April `{python} drift_april` to `{python} num(ex_c[-1], 2)` and `{python} num(ex_e[-1], 2)` in those for April `{python} c4_last_april`, with earnings at `{python} num(ex_e[e_peak], 2)` for April `{python} DR["determination_years"][e_peak] + 1`. Removing each year's mean error lowers the mean share in `{python} fy(FINAL)` by `{python} points(GAPS["re_centring_part"], 2)` points (@tbl-c4-decomp).

The second model's inputs vary more than the baseline model's, and the saving rises with that variation. Across the Aprils `{python} c4_first_april` to `{python} c4_last_april` its statutory inputs have standard deviations of `{python} num(sd_c4["cpi"][0], 1)` to `{python} num(sd_c4["cpi"][1], 1)` points for CPI and `{python} num(sd_c4["earnings"][0], 1)` to `{python} num(sd_c4["earnings"][1], 1)` for earnings, against `{python} num(sd_sc["cpi"][0], 1)` to `{python} num(sd_sc["cpi"][1], 1)` and `{python} num(sd_sc["earnings"][0], 1)` to `{python} num(sd_sc["earnings"][1], 1)` on the earnings scenarios' paths. The errors for `{python} late[0]` to `{python} late[-1]` enter years five to twelve of `{python} pct(100 * RES["share_paths_years_5_12_use_a_late_target_year"], 0)` of the paths. Scaling every error down lowers the mean share roughly in proportion, and calendar-year errors in place of the statutory ones give a lower share (@tbl-c4-decomp). The `{python} FLOOR` floor raises the share more on the second model's paths than on the earnings scenarios': without it, the difference between the second model's mean share in `{python} fy(FINAL)` and the average of the two earnings scenarios' shares (@tbl-scenarios) falls from `{python} points(GAPS["with_floor"], 1)` to `{python} points(GAPS["floor_off"], 1)` points, with the scenarios' shares without the floor estimated, in rule arithmetic, on their sampled paths.

Output of a model that failed its registered test, not a probability statement."

```{python}
        ("Calendar-year errors in place of statutory ones", DC["calendar_errors"]),
```

@tbl-c4-scores gives every score of the second model on both tests, with April 2022 scored as in law. Among the sensitivities that the registration named, which do not enter the verdict, the model without the draw of the average error and without the small-sample correction would have met every check; the rule forbids promoting it. The other three would have failed. With pools of earlier forecasts only, which the registration scores on the seven-forecast test, `{python} words(chr_a["hits"])` of `{python} words(chr_a["n"])` four-year outcomes fall inside the central 80% band, and the plausible range of `{python} pct(100 * chr_a["wilson95_independent"][0], 0)` to `{python} pct(100 * chr_a["wilson95_independent"][1], 0)` excludes 80%. With leave-one-forecast-out pools the floor bias on the seven-forecast test is `{python} num(loo_fb, 3)`, and two other checks fail: the score ratio for lead changes on the seven-forecast test, `{python} num(float(loo_rest[0][2]), 3)`, and the count of four-year gaps inside the band that holds the middle half of the paths on the thirteen-forecast test, `{python} words(int(loo_rest[1][2]))` of `{python} words(n_c4)`. With raw errors, neither de-meaned nor shifted by a draw of the average error, `{python} words(len(RAW))` checks fail, among them a floor bias of `{python} num(raw_fb, 3)` on the seven-forecast test.

```{python}

The three added checks apply to the thirteen-forecast test only. A dash marks a check not applied."

body += [
```

## Appendix: example pensioners {#sec-examples .appendix}

```{python}
exs = D.examples(D.path(EXP))
ex_rows = [(k, ex, D.borne_share(ex, FINAL)) for k, ex in exs.items()]
ex = dict(exs)
gc_years_a = [y for y in D.YEARS if D.ex_change(ex["owner"], "guarantee_credit", y) > 0.5]
sc_d = -D.ex_change(ex["basic_renter"], "savings_credit", FINAL)
hb_c = D.ex_change(ex["social_renter"], "housing_benefit", FINAL)
```

Four hypothetical pensioners, run as households under each rule on the model path near the median gap, show how tax and benefits pass on a lower State Pension (@tbl-pensioners, @fig-pensioners); the OBR long-term run carries no example households, and the model path carries no probability weight. Each receives the full flat-rate State Pension and, unlike the survey runs, claims every benefit it is entitled to. A lower State Pension means less income tax for a pensioner above the personal allowance and more Pension Credit for one entitled to it; Pension Credit counts income after tax [@spc2002], and council tax reduction disregards the income of a pensioner receiving the guarantee credit [@si2012_2885]. The last row of @tbl-pensioners gives the share of the lower pension that reaches each pensioner's income in `{python} fy(FINAL)`.

Thresholds explain the differences, and two modelling conventions set the thresholds (@sec-model). The Pension Credit guarantee rises with earnings under both rules, and the personal allowance stays at `{python} V2['personal_allowance']` to `{python} fy(V2['pa_frozen_to'])` and then rises with CPI, so the full new State Pension is above the allowance and taxed once the rules can differ. With only the full new State Pension, a pensioner sits close to the Pension Credit guarantee after tax. Under the adjusted rule the pensioner (a) therefore receives more guarantee credit than under the triple lock in some years (`{python} listing([fy(y) for y in gc_years_a])`), and with it more council tax reduction. In those years benefits make up more of the lower pension, so the line in @fig-pensioners moves from year to year. The pensioner with a `{python} gbp(ex["private_pension"]["meta"]["private_pension"])` private pension (b) is above every threshold and bears most of the loss, less income tax. The council tenant (c) is better off under the adjusted rule in `{python} fy(FINAL)` because of a cliff: the lower pension takes the tenant onto the guarantee credit, which passports maximum Housing Benefit, `{python} gbp(hb_c)` a year more, and full council tax reduction, and together with less income tax these more than make up the lower pension. The survey-wide results cannot reproduce such a gain, because there Housing Benefit and council tax reduction respond only for households already receiving them (@sec-model). The older pensioner on the basic State Pension (d) receives the guarantee credit under both rules: extra guarantee credit makes up the lower pension in full, but they receive `{python} gbp(sc_d)` less savings credit. Whether (a) and (c) reach the guarantee credit depends on the conventions: if the Pension Credit guarantee instead rose by the same percentage as the State Pension under each rule, if the personal allowance were higher or if a successor to the Pension Tax Allowance removed their income tax, they would be less likely to cross it, and (a) and (c) would lose the income tax offset.
